With disposable cameras, the end of the frame counter marks the conclusion of its journey. But the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera offers an odyssey, or possibly even, a never-ending story with its reloadable function. Having that potential for boundless reuse also means a chance to get crazily creative with your rolls.

In this tipster, we've put together a complete guide comparing a range of Lomography film stocks using the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera. We're covering everything from the warmth of the LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 and the dramatic mood of the LomoChrome Metropolis ISO 100–400, to the surreal color shifts of the LomoChrome Purple Pétillant ISO 100–400 and the timeless charm of Lady Grey B&W ISO 400.

As a bonus, we’ve also added a mini gallery featuring the LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed ISO 400, Lomography Color Negative 800 and Lomography Redscale XR ISO 50–200, to help you find the right roll that matches your style.

Street Photography

When using the LomoChrome Classicolor for street photography, expect your photos to appear very lively and vivid. It has a colorful, rich, and warm quality that is ideal for when you want to capture the joy of everyday scenes outdoors especially during sunny days! LomoChrome Metropolis is also great match for this genre of photography as it can truly capture the raw character of urban spaces and industrial surroundings. The film’s strong contrast highlights architectural details and produces a gritty, documentary-like energy to photos.

  • !Image 6
  • !Image 7
  • !Image 8
  • !Image 9

Credits: Elisa Parrino | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200, LomoChrome Metropolis 35 mm ISO 100–400, LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400, &Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

Meanwhile, Lady Grey B&W ISO 400 simplifies the chaos of the streets by stripping everything back into timeless monochromatic frames reminiscent of classic film photography. Opt for black and white when you want to simply observe the interplay of light, texture, and composition of your photos. A complete opposite of that is the LomoChrome Purple, the film that takes you on an otherworldly journey with its surreal color shifts. It's the boldest option and rewards street photographers who aren't afraid to experiment and embrace peculiarity like purple trees and mint skies!

Portrait Photography

If you’re aiming to get natural-looking skin tones, LomoChrome Classicolor feels the most appropriate out of the four. Using this film gives your images a balanced color palette and creates warm tones without oversaturating. LomoChrome Metropolis has a moodier approach, taking away the scene’s saturation and increasing contrast for dramatic portraits.

Being a black-and-white film, Lady Grey B&W ISO 400 exudes the timeless charm of vintage portraits – deep shadows, high tonal range, fine grain. Without color competing for attention, this film emphasizes the facial features and emotion of your subject/s. Finally, LomoChrome Purple offers a unique approach to portrait photography if you want to push things a bit further. It has a color-shifting effect that turns your subject’s skin tones into a different hue and makes them glow with an unconventional look.

  • !Image 18
  • !Image 19
  • !Image 20
  • !Image 21

Credits: Sunsern Poontavee, Elisa Parrino & Guilia Ciampi | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200, LomoChrome Metropolis 35 mm ISO 100–400, LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400, &Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

When your subject is set against a wider backdrop, the films’ distinct styles become even more apparent, creating different atmospheres for your subject to blend with.

LomoChrome Classicolor renders brightly colored backgrounds beautifully – buildings, walls, staircases, storefronts, floral fields, and trees. The film’s color palette naturally creates harmony between the subject and the background especially in well-lit shooting environments. On the contrary, LomoChrome Metropolis softens colors and tames the overall scene, perfect for when you want a subdued, grunge-like setting.

  • !Image 22
  • !Image 23
  • !Image 24
  • !Image 25

Credits: Tony Sotelo, Nate Soriano, Kota Sekiya & Elisa Parrino | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200, LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400, Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400, &LomoChrome Metropolis 35 mm ISO 100–400

Still-Life Photography

Contrasting the spontaneity of street photography are stills, and the Half-Frame camera makes a versatile companion to capture both subjects in motion and objects at rest. Beginning with the LomoChrome Classicolor, colors seem more vibrant and naturally saturated with a slightly warm tint. Contrast and highlights blend nicely evoking an overall sunny garden mood as seen in the flora subject.

Striking a cooler alternative are photos on LomoChrome Metropolis evoking a ‘hazy disposition’. Tones are flatter, as seen in the muted greens and reds in the captured foliage. LomoChrome Purple flips the spectrum, turning verdure into varying shades of purple creating an otherworldly atmosphere. Lastly, photos taken on Lady Grey B&W ISO 400 render a park scene straight from a black and white film. Generally, colors on the Half-frame camera are punchy, especially in outdoor photos taken in broad daylight.

  • !Image 26

The next set of photos features objects in lower light, although still taken during the day. Surprisingly, colors retain their pop despite the canopy. This is most noticeable on the yellow post box, wherein colors range from bright yellow on LomoChrome Classicolor to a shade of fuchsia on LomoChrome Purple.

Overall, the Half-Frame camera makes a great match for capturing stills, especially for those on the spur moment shots during a quiet Sunday stroll through the park or a light city trek across the urban jungle.

More Half-Frame Film Recommendations for Your Photography Style

Looking to reload the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera with something new? Check out our short list of recommendations to match the mood of your next photo run.

Lomography Color Negative ISO 800 – Best for Night Life Photographers

Thinking of spicing up those party shots from a night out on the block? Lock and reload your Half-Frame camera with Lomography Color Negative ISO 800. Bold colors and gorgeous grain make it the right fit for nightlife photographers looking to close the distance on who or whatever they’re shooting. Pair this quick roll with a flash to assure that there’s never a dull moment.

Lomography Redscale XR ISO 50–200 – Best for Experimental Photographers

Drowning your photos in a warm sea of red, orange, and yellow, the Redscale XR ISO 50–200 imbues a certain grunge similar to the album cover of Soundgarden’s ‘Superunknown’. If experimental portraits are your style, then reloading the half-frame with this color shifting role will guarantee a certain rawness and intensity to those atmospheric photoshoots. Bring the heat and let loose with this film stock.

LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed ISO 400 – Best for Lifestyle Photographers

If you treat a simple trip to the park like a runway for your outfit details, try the LomoChrome Sun-Kissed ISO 400 – made for lifestyle photographers who love creating visual diaries. Its color palette gives a nostalgic, retro feel that uniquely captures light and color with style. While it works magnificently under the sun to make your subjects glow, this film’s versatile nature surely won’t keep you from documenting a casual day out in the city. Pair it with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera to get chic diptychs with your friends!

For this edition of Analogue Journal, we invited Chadaporn Jaiman, also known as Lin (linnpingg_, and lintistart) to share a series of instant photographs that capture the little moments of everyday life – from her favorite hobbies to the simple moments that bring her joy. She also expressed her personality and imagination by painting the Lomo'Instant in her own unique style, turning the camera itself into a creative canvas, and journaling her experience in the Soft Cover Album.

Let's take a look at her heartwarming photographs and discover the stories behind them.

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) with the Lomo'Instant

Hi, Lin! Welcome to Lomography Magazine. Could you introduce yourself and tell us a little about what you've been up to lately?

Hi! I'm Chadaporn Jaiman, or you can call me Lin. I'm 20 years old. I'd describe myself as friendly and easy to get along with, even though I'm somewhat of an introvert. I smile a lot and always find joy in the little things around me, especially painting. I've been working as a model for almost four years now, and I'm currently studying Fine Arts with a focus on painting.

I feel that these two paths complement each other in a really meaningful way, allowing me to grow both creatively and personally. I'm also someone who gets deeply immersed in the things I love, whether it's art, new experiences, or anything that inspires me.

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) using the Lomo'Instant&Soft Cover Album

> Translation: I'm painting on the canvas right now, but I'm not ready to show it yet. For now, you'll just have to enjoy my smile!

Have you ever kept a journal like this before?

Honestly, this is my first time. Normally, I like to preserve happy memories through photographs, so keeping a journal like this was a completely new experience for me. Since it was my first try, I wanted it to reflect my personality as much as possible.

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) using the Lomo'Instant&Soft Cover Album

> Translation: I still don't know what to paint! Here's a smile for you first! | Anyway, the atmosphere is so nice. It's the rainy season – the trees must be loving it!

How did it feel to document your everyday life in a more analogue way like this?

It made life feel slower and more analogue. I found myself becoming more present and paying closer attention to what was right in front of me. It gave me the chance to spend real offline time with myself – painting, listening to the sounds of nature, and appreciating all the little moments happening around me.

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) using the Lomo'Instant&Soft Cover Album

> Translation: The painting is finished! I still haven't painted the camera yet, so here's the unfinished version first.

How has instant photography changed the way you capture and preserve your memories?

Instant photography captures a moment exactly as it is. It feels like a memory preserved on a single piece of film, complete with its own mood and color palette that always brings a sense of nostalgia whenever I look back at it. What makes it so much more special than taking photos with a phone is that there's only one original print in the world. The soft blur, light leaks, and other little imperfections become part of its charm. Every time I hold an instant photo again, I'm reminded not only of what I saw, but also of the atmosphere, the laughter, and even the warmth and happiness I felt in that exact moment.

  • !Image 5
  • !Image 6

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) using the Lomo'Instant&Soft Cover Album

> Translation: A delicious quick snack while painting. Such a nice little moment! | This is my selfie, not sure how it'll turn out though.

> Translation: A nice dinner to reward myself! The sweet and sour stir-fry was so good! Luckily I took a photo before finishing it, otherwise you wouldn't have seen it! ><

Do you have a favorite photo or journal page? Could you tell us about it?

I honestly love every photo, but if I had to choose just one, it would be this one. As for the story behind it...you'll have to check out the journal page to find out!

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) using the Lomo'Instant&Soft Cover Album

> Translation: This is my favorite photo because it was the last one I took after dinner at the Train Night Market. I left with a full stomach and a heart full of happiness.

We invited you to paint your own camera. Could you tell us a little about the concept behind your design?

When I first started painting on the camera, I wasn't sure what I wanted to create. That uncertainty naturally turned into loose, chaotic lines that felt a little messy and unstructured. But within that chaos, I added flowers and a minimal color palette that reflects who I am. In the end, it became a concept I like to call “Chaos in Bloom”.

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) using the Lomo'Instant&Soft Cover Album

> Translation: “Chaos in Bloom”. That's what I called it because I was so indecisive about what to paint at first. But once it was finished, I ended up loving it so much. I'm super proud of it! Haha.

Credits: Lin (linnpingg__) using the Lomo'Instant&Soft Cover Album

Where can people follow your work?

You can find my artwork on Instagram at lintistart. It's a space where I share a collection of my paintings over the years. Although I don't post every single piece, each work I choose to share holds a special place in my heart. You can also follow me at linnpingg_, where I share my modeling work with different photographers, along with little stories and everyday moments that I'd love to share with everyone.

A big thank you to Lin for sharing these quiet, everyday moments through her instant photographs, and for giving the Lomo'Instant camera her own creative touch with a one-of-a-kind hand-painted design. We hope her story inspires you to slow down, embrace the analogue process, and find beauty in the little moments that make each day special.

Music is visual.Martinus Ragita is a professional Indonesian stage and concert photographer who translates the raw energy, rhythm, and atmosphere of live performances into timeless frames. He serves as the primary photographer for several of Indonesia's biggest contemporary music acts, including .Feast, Hindia, Lomba Sihir, and breakout pop star Bernadya.

We sent two rolls of the LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400 and Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400. He wasted no time and dove straight into the world of Lomography.

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

Hi, Martinus! It’s great to have you here at Lomography! Tell us about yourself. What do you do? What are some of your interests?

Hi Lomography, happy to be here! I’m a photographer based in Jakarta, mostly focused on music/stage photography, though I love jumping between portrait, couple, and street photography, too – honestly, anything that catches my attention, especially people, as subjects.

  • !Image 2
  • !Image 3
  • !Image 4
  • !Image 5

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

What made you start taking photos?

At first, it was just for fun back in elementary school when I borrowed my relative’s camera. It slowly became a hobby throughout middle and high school, then turned into my passion and work during college. I just really love capturing moments that will never happen again, and knowing people can hold onto those memories through my photos makes me happy.

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

What's your favorite thing about analogue photography?

That I can’t really recreate the same character and effects with a digital camera. I also love the whole process – from taking the photo to finally seeing the results. It feels exciting every time, like a small adrenaline rush.

“I like LomoChrome Purple! It gives such a funky and eclectic feel without needing much editing or color grading.”

How do you describe your photography? Do you have any film photographers that you look up to?

I don’t think I have one specific style, but my photos have always been about people and moments that not everyone notices. I also love experimenting with colors and lighting whenever I get the chance. As for inspirations, I look up to Martin Parr and Trevor Roberts a lot.

  • !Image 7
  • !Image 8
  • !Image 9
  • !Image 10
  • !Image 11

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

What's it like to be Martinus these days? How do you spend your week?

On weekdays, wake up early, go to the gym, run, sometimes play pickleball with friends, and spend my time editing photos. On weekends, I mostly travel and work with musicians during their concerts, so it feels like working and traveling at the same time.

  • !Image 12
  • !Image 13
  • !Image 14
  • !Image 15
  • !Image 16

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

What is it like to be a photographer in Jakarta? Please tell us your experience.

Jakarta is hectic, loud, and fast-paced, so being a photographer here can get pretty tiring. But the city is full of energy, and there’s always easy access to events, communities, and creative opportunities.

“...love the whole process – from taking the photo to finally seeing the results. It feels exciting every time, like a small adrenaline rush.”

What did you decide to shoot with the LomoChrome Purple?

I used it to experiment with some shots during Lomba Sihir’s stage at the Bla Bla Bla Fest in Pontianak.

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

What did you like the most about this film stock?

It really stands out. I rarely see colors like these in other films. It gives such a funky and eclectic feel without needing much editing or color grading.

  • !Image 18
  • !Image 19
  • !Image 20

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

Was there one photo from this shoot that stood out to you? What makes it special?

I got a photo of Enrico, Lomba Sihir's drummer. He was about to eat, but somehow he fell asleep. It was a really unusual and funny moment, and that's why the photo stands out to me.

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

And how about the Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400? Was it your first time using this film?

Yes, it was my first time using it, and I really liked it. It’s not your usual black-and-white film. It has more texture and sharpness, which makes the photos feel more alive.

© Martinus Ragita using Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400

If this photo series had a soundtrack, which song would you choose to capture its spirit?

Probably something from Bleachers, You and Forever.

  • !Image 23
  • !Image 24
  • !Image 25
  • !Image 26
  • !Image 27
  • !Image 28
  • !Image 29

© Martinus Ragita using Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400

What is one thing you have been dying to explore further (anything from a place to a particular subject)? What's your dream project?

I’d love to shoot an international music festival or concert someday. One of my biggest dreams is to photograph my favorite artists live on stage.

“...I just really love capturing moments that will never happen again, and knowing people can hold onto those memories through my photos makes me happy.”

Tell us about some of the current projects you are working on. Do you have any projects in particular you are looking forward to?

Right now, I’m working with a few Indonesian musicians, capturing their moments on stage as usual. I’m also really looking forward to future overseas trips with them.

© Martinus Ragita using LomoChrome Purple Pétillant 35 mm ISO 100–400

What’s coming up on the horizon? What’s in the works and what’s on your mind?

I’m looking forward to growing more through my work, trying new things, and continuing to capture moments that make people feel something.

  • !Image 31
  • !Image 32
  • !Image 33
  • !Image 34

© Martinus Ragita using Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400

Any messages to Lomographers out there?

Keep experimenting and find your own colors.

Thank you, Martinus, for sharing his photos, knowledge, and experiences with us all! Keep up with his latest work on Instagram and portfolio on his website.

https://www.lomography.com/magazine/3589.content:
We’ve been to Vienna, Paris and Milan in our Now & Then series, where we use archival film photos and give them a certain Lomographic flair. We now find ourselves in London, a city technically classified as a forest, one with the oldest subway in the world, and where over 300 languages are spoken. I took along a few photos as inspiration, my Lomomatic 110 and Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, to recreate history.

I journeyed to London on the first weekend of May for the concert of none other than Miss Olivia Dean. Given that it was my first time in the city, of course, I had to make the most of it. Over the four days that we were there, I walked a total of 95,505 steps through one of the coolest cities I have ever been to.

While I took along a few photos that I had hoped to perfectly recreate, nothing went according to plan. It was my first time in the city, so I was looking at everything through a fresh perspective, without knowledge of where certain sites were and how to capture them in the perfect angle. That being said, this is what Lomography is all about. We capture life around us through its chaos and perfect imperfection. So what I present to you, dear reader, are a few side-by-side comparisons and my impressions of a city that I would return to again and again.

I touched down in London at around 9 in the morning on a Saturday. After setting up at a hotel near St. Pancras Train Station, we headed into the city to grab a bite at one of the most bustling spots I've experienced: Borough Market. What began as a trading hub on the south bank of the Thames in 1014 is now full of mouth-watering food options and over 100 stalls.

Borough Market

[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/angelinatacinelli/photos/29466293)

Now: Borough Market | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

What I love about the Lomomatic 110 is that you can never say for certain what will come out in your frames. The lens is slightly askew from where the viewfinder is, which works as a built-in experimental option. The photo I took in Borough Market is one of my favorites. First off, the partially exposed sprocket and lightened portion of the frame add a certain something I could not have recreated if I wanted to.

Most of the photos, if not all, I captured without thinking. I truly took the don’t think, just shoot concept to heart, which is what makes them sort of like my own personal diary.

Leadenhall Market

[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/angelinatacinelli/photos/29615140)

Now: Close-Up of Leadenhall Market | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

Next up on our journey was Leadenhall Market, where I happened to have the best latte of my life, and of course, for Potterheads, where Chris Columbus filmed the first Harry Potter film. The red hues of the restaurants and interior of the market jumped out to me, and the Color Tiger ISO 200 film also perfectly captured it.

Oxford Circus

[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/angelinatacinelli/photos/29466300)

Now: Oxford Circus | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

The next day, we hopped off the Tube at Oxford Circus Station, the busiest shopping street in all of Europe. The area has around 300 shops and more than 72,000 people step through every day. The “circus” layout was designed in the 19th century to best facilitate traffic movement.

I found this sign right in the center, and had to time the shot perfectly because the name of the station flashed on and off. Given that I was in the shopping center of Europe, I also had to pick up a few things, like one-too-many Jellycats.

The National Gallery

  • !Image 4
  • !Image 5

Then: London, National Gallery 1955 - 1955 - Sörmland Museum, Sweden - CC BY-SA | Now: View of the National Gallery, Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

I am nothing if not an art nerd, so, of course, I had to pay a visit to the National Gallery, a museum with over 2,300 masterpieces in Trafalgar Square. This is one of the spots where I managed to frame the Now & Then photos correctly, and almost everything is the same – give or take a generation and a few columns added.

I love the comparison of the dresses of those going about their day. Once inside the museum, it was room after room of stunningly captivating pieces, one of my favorites being The Execution of Lady Jane Grey, painted by Paul Delaroche.

Notting Hill

  • !Image 6[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/angelinatacinelli/photos/29466295)
  • !Image 7[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/angelinatacinelli/photos/29466294)

Now: View of Notting Hill | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

By the end of the day, we were buzzed on life in London (and maybe something else) and ended up in Notting Hill – an artsy neighborhood known for its pastel-colored homes, and one-a-well-known-rom-com was maybe filmed here.

We went right around sunset, and the lighting conditions were a great fit for the 200 ISO. One of my friends took over with shooting the photos, which I feel brought a new perspective and funky feeling to the frames.

St. James Park

[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/angelinatacinelli/photos/29466304)

Now: St. James Park | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

St. James Park has an interesting history – what started as a leper hospital was transformed by the infamous Henry VIII into a park in 1532. The pelicans (friendly or not) have been living there for almost 350 years. We strolled around the grounds, and I took this photo after seeing a batch of Irises (my favorite flower) growing by the water.

The photo I took is my own version of an impressionist painting, en plein air, inspired by what was around me. I remember the wind rustling through the trees as we walked along the paths on our last day in London, and this moment in the park took me out of the bustling city and into a moment of stillness.

Buckingham Palace

  • !Image 9
  • !Image 10

Then: Grup Turístic - 1974 by El Centre - Digital Memory of Catalonia, Spain - Public Domain | Now: Buckingham Palace, Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

Buckingham Palace is probably one of the most recognizable buildings in all of London and serves as the main symbol of the British Monarchy. With 775 rooms, a balcony where everything from wars to weddings has been announced, and a plentiful 78 bathrooms to choose from, it was also a lovely photographic subject.

My favorite part about the photos is the Victoria Memorial monument as the golden shades came up beautifully on my film roll. Once again, the framing was not perfect, but the area remains mainly unchanged, aside from the lovely outfits and means of transportation.

Westminster Abbey

  • !Image 11
  • !Image 12

Then: "Westminster Abbey, London", c. 1843, Rijksmuseum, P-F-00-2429 | Now: Close-Up of Westminster Abbey, Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

Westminster Abbey just sounds fancy, and it is. Since 1066, 40 British monarchs have been crowned there and a poet corner honors several old writers that you may have been forced to read in English class. It is right in the center of London and has seen several transformations in its lifetime.

The framing of the photo was difficult to get “right” but I feel like the difference in photos are a nod to its dynamic history. I took the photo vertically with my Lomomatic 110 which allowed for more detail in the frame.

Big Ben

  • !Image 13
  • !Image 14

Then: London, Westminster Palace, Elizabeth Tower: Uhrturm (auch gen. Big Ben) by Barry, Charles (1795-1860) (Künstler/Hersteller) - Media library of Art and Visual History of Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany - CC BY-SA | Now: Big Ben Detail, | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 Camera&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200, May 2026

Perhaps my favorite photo from the trip was of Big Ben. I recently learned that the name actually refers to the bell inside, which weighs an extremely light 13.7 tons. The tower is the height of 21 London buses stacked upon each other, and has a wonderfully unique bell ring as it cracked in 1858, giving it its signature sound.

Both the photos capture it as it stands tall above the skyline, give or take a lovely lamp pole. This was one of our last stops on our trip, and it seems like we saved the best for last.

A Classy Cheerio

Life never goes according to plan, and neither does film photography. From fumbled frames to imperfections in the development of a film roll, we never know how our photos are going to turn out. I went to London with a plan to recreate some old photos (and eat my weight in Fish and Chips), but the results were not what I expected.

At Lomography, we learn to live through and with the chaos. We capture life as it is, and those unforeseen moments in between are the best kind. I encourage you to find what inspires you – whether it is recreating old photos or making new memories of your own. Go out into this world fearlessly. Oh, and don’t forget your film camera, of course.

Keep an eye out for new cities in the series, and if you have recreated your own photographs, send them to us at [travel@lomography.com](mailto:travel@lomography.com).

Levana Cynthia is a professional wedding photographer from Indonesia whose photography portfolio is primarily built around destination weddings, couple sessions, and travel photography. She operates under creative brand Calvin & Levana alongside her husband, Calvin, and on her personal platform, shares her solo travel photography adventures.

She regularly travels to capture local cultures, street scenes, wildlife, and natural phenomena, with her curated journals covering trips across Japan, Vietnam, India, the United States, and the United Kingdom. Luckily for us, when we sent her a Petzval Art Lens, she was just about to board to India.

  • !Image 1
  • !Image 2

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

Hi, Levana. It’s great to have you here at Lomography! Tell us about yourself. What do you do and what are some of your interests??

Hi! I’m a professional Wedding Photographer. My biggest hobby is, of course, photography. I love spending time outdoors, especially in nature. I also enjoy running!

  • !Image 3
  • !Image 4

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

What's it like to be Levana these days? How do you spend your week?

Weekends are usually wedding days for me! When I finally get a bit of free time, I like to go for a run or just get outside and enjoy some fresh air. Being in nature is my favorite way to recharge.

“I think the bokeh is what really sets this lens apart. It's something I haven't experienced with any other lens.”

How do you describe your photography?

I love photographing couples and capturing the connection between them, the kind of emotion you can actually feel through a photo. My style is natural, candid, and moment-driven. I don't like over-directing them. I prefer creating a comfortable space where they can just be themselves, and that's when the best moments happen.

Do you have any photographers that you look up to?

Yes, I really admire Carol Kuntjoro.

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

We sent you a Petzval Lens to try out. What were your first impressions, and in what ways does using this lens differ from your usual photographic method?

This lens is really unique. Even though I'm used to shooting with manual lenses, this one still felt completely different. Besides focusing manually, I can also control the shape of the bokeh, which makes the whole shooting experience a lot more fun and creative.

Tell us your thoughts on Lomography's Petzval Art Lens. What is your favorite feature or characteristic of the Art Lens?

I honestly love the vibe this lens creates. Everything feels so moody and dreamy, almost like a scene from a dream. The bokeh is really unique.

How did it feel to shoot with it?

It was really fun. Even when I used it for street photography, I couldn't rush my shots. I had to slow down, take my time to get the focus right, and wait for the right mood. I actually really enjoyed that process.

  • !Image 6
  • !Image 7

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

Could you tell us about the locations and stories behind these photographs taken with the Petzval Art Lens?

I brought this lens with me on my trips to India and the US. Both places were busy, crowded, and a little chaotic, but somehow this lens made everything feel calmer. It helped me slow down and capture a softer, more peaceful vibe, even in the middle of all the chaos.

  • !Image 8
  • !Image 9
  • !Image 10

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

Do you have a favorite shot from your experience with the Petzval Art Lens? Why that photo?

[This photo] just feels right. It almost feels like you're inside a dream. The bokeh, the light...everything has this soft, warm, dreamy feeling. And the people in the frame look like they've just reunited with someone they've been waiting to see for a long time.

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

Where do you think is the most suitable outdoor location for the Petzval Art Lens?

Honestly, it works pretty much anywhere. But I think it looks even better during golden hour, in a moody setting, or somewhere with lots of lights.

  • !Image 12
  • !Image 13
  • !Image 14

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

What do you think sets this lens apart from others?

I think the bokeh is what really sets this lens apart. It's something I haven't experienced with any other lens.

Do you have any tips or tricks for shooting with the Art Lens?

Don't rush it. Take your time, experiment with the settings, and find the vibe that works for you.

“I honestly love the vibe this lens creates. Everything feels so moody and dreamy, almost like a scene from a dream.”

What is one thing you have been dying to explore further (anything from a place to a particular subject)? What is your dream project?

I'd love to document local cultures and everyday life in remote places. I also want to explore landscapes that are completely different from where I live, like Iceland.

Tell us about some of the current projects you are working on. Do you have any projects in particular you are looking forward to?

Most of my work right now consists of weddings and couple shoots. Honestly, I'm excited every time I have a shoot because every couple is different. They all have their own personalities and chemistry, so I always get to explore different vibes and capture each story in a unique way.

  • !Image 15
  • !Image 16

© Levana Cynthia using the Petzval 55 mm f/1.7 Art Lens

Any messages to other Lomographers out there?

Don't be afraid to try new things, like experimenting with different lenses! Every lens has its own character, and it's always fun to discover what you can create with it.

Thank you, Levana, for sharing her photos, thoughts, and experiences with us all! Keep up with his latest work on her Instagram.

https://www.lomography.com/magazine/3589.content:
You remember that feeling of the last day before summer vacation, sitting in your last class of the day, the entire student body buzzing? When half of your peers hadn't bothered to show up, and the other half count down the minutes, no seconds, until the clock strikes summer – that moment you've been working towards all year?

Now, let’s go back a few hundred years, to a world where apparently only men can get an education, everyone smelled a lot worse, and paintings were the only way to see the world around you. The grandiose Grand Tour was taken by young men (perhaps the sixth Alexander in their family) across Europe, as a way to experience the whole wide world (a.k.a. homogeneous European countries), and live the dolce vita lifestyle.

For this historical piece, we will go into the early history of travel photography, from inspirations in painting to the use of portable cameras. From sipping on a glass of vin in France to “discovering” Greek ruins, we will traverse through space and time, with, of course, a little Lomographic flair. You know the phrase what happens on vacation, stays on vacation? We will see how true that is.

  • !Image 1
  • !Image 2

Left: Portrait of a Young Man. Pompeo Batoni, ca. 1760–65. Oil on canvas. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Object Number 03.37.1 | Right: Ancient Rome. Giovanni Paolo Panini, 1757. Oil on canvas. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Object Number 52.63.1

Setting the Scene

Imagine yourself as an English chap. The year is 1780. Day after day, you sit in an English boarding school, or in your oversized estate with a private tutor, learning about philosophy, science, and maybe a bit of Economics, as Adam Smith has just published The Wealth of Nations a few years prior. Bored by the fact that your biggest problem is that you have to take over the estate once your father is no longer walking the sweet green grass of this Earth, you decide to set off on a journey so unbelievable, you will brag about it for years to come.

Yes, while any other person in the working class had to work all month to earn a fraction of what you spend in a day, you decide to jet off on an all-expenses-paid trip across the English Channel, through France, Italy, and with the final destination of Greece. The journey excites and delights you, and the prospect of being free from the chains of aristocratic life is truly tantalizing. This is the Grand Tour, the beginning of travel as we know it today.

Image: Italian Picture Dealers Humbugging My Lord Anglaise. Thomas Rowlandson, May 30, 1812. Hand-colored etching. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Object Number 59.533.1221

Painting on the Road

Until this point, the only way to see the world was through paintings. Artists such as Canaletto and Bellotto created masterful landscapes of cities, such as Dresden, Vienna, and Venice. Some of these paintings make their way back into England, as King George III had begun amassing a large collection of them. Photography did not exist, so you could either patronize a painting of a city that lives in your dreams, or see it for yourself.

Most of those who embarked on this Grand Tour were young, aristocratic lads between the ages of 18 and 25. Free from the borders of their hometowns, and, I guess, stuffy society, it was the first time they could let loose and drink all the wine they wanted. Think Colin Bridgerton, from the Bridgerton series on Netflix.

What they journey to find is something beyond the paintings, beyond the whispers of the languages that others have experienced. They want to find a new version of themselves, have lots of sex without consequences, and find a way to capture it.

Image: Landscape with Travellers, Two Riding in a Carriage Driven by a Postilion and a Third on Horseback behind. Marco Ricci, about 1720. Pen and brown ink with brown wash, over black chalk. The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, Object Number 95.GG.24

Across the English Channel We Go

The first stop for many was France after a voyage across the English Channel, into a port city such as Calais or Le Havre. Once there, the men hired a French-speaking guide and secured a private carriage to Paris. There, they spent months experiencing the city and mingling with French girls.

British tourists often complained about 18th-century French food, the lack of comfort during their inn stays, and the extremely pleasant sewage that dotted the streets of Paris. However, for any young aristocrat hoping to go into government or diplomacy, it was a necessary step in refining their tastes and learning the language of romance and unpronounced letters, French.

  • !Image 5
  • !Image 6

Bernardo Bellotto (Italian, 1722 - 1780). View of the Grand Canal: Santa Maria della Salute and the Dogana from Campo Santa Maria Zobenigo, about 1743. Oil on canvas. The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, 91.PA.73 | Right: Piazza San Marco. Canaletto, late 1720s. Oil on canvas. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Object Number 1988.162

An Italian Passegiatta

Next up on this grand escapade for most of our partiers, oh wait, I mean serious, distinguished travelers, was Italy. Along with their trusty carriage driver and steed who most certainly deserved a break, they would spend months, and sometimes years, exploring cities such as Venice, Rome, and Florence.

They entered Italy via the Alps, and crossed the Brenner or Mont Cenis passes. From walking through the Roman ruins, to admiring Renaissance art, these itineraries formed the very early cornerstones of what drives travel today. They commissioned portraits by local artists, such as Pompeo Batoni, and collected vedute, or cityscape paintings, as souvenirs.

Galivanting on a Greek Adventure

Many Grand Tours took the most adventurous turn in Greece, where travelers explored rugged terrain to see legendary sites such as Mycenae, Epidaurus, and the Olympic stadium in Olympia. Of course, their feet also stepped onto the Acropolis and the Parthenon, as they were inspired by the thousands of years of democracy and philosophy around them.

During this era of an I saw it first culture in a pre-photography world, the cost of these trips was a small price to pay to study the works of Michelangelo or sit and sketch the ancient ruins in Greece. This was the earliest form of traveling for leisure, and the only thing missing? A way to capture it almost instantly.

  • !Image 7
  • !Image 8

Left: Santa Lucia, Naples. Calvert Richard Jones, 1845–46. Salted paper prints from paper negatives. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Object Number 2005.100.562 | Right: Interno del Colosseo. Giovanni Battista Altadonna, 1850s. Albumen silver print from glass negative. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Object Number 2005.100.562

Early Travel Photography

Forms of documentation changed when photography hit the scene a few decades later in 1839. No, instead of commissioning portraits and supporting local artists, now, these early travelers could capture their own awakenings with a camera.

Two photography processes were announced in 1839 that completely changed travel (and the world) as we knew it: the daguerreotype and the photogenic drawing. In the beginning, photography was not the most practical; the photographs took a while, and the cameras were large and not very portable. Professional bookshops and printers set up shops in major European cities that created photographic souvenirs and postcards.

Later processes like albumen printing, while producing much better results, still demanded a fresh supply of eggs at all times for the coating. Some even traveled with a few friendly chickens, which sure made for some fun (and maybe smelly) development!

  • !Image 9
  • !Image 10

Credits: Reisefotos Griechenland. Rhodos (Stadt). Travel photos of Greece. Rhodes (town). Tourist with an 8 mm camera on a tripod filming, presumably in the Aigos fortress. In the background, a partial view of the passenger ship "Milwaukee" by Grasser, Franz (Herstellung) (Fotograf) - Deutsche Fotothek, Germany - Public Domain | Reisefotos Griechenland. Travel photos of Greece. Tourist with a 8mm camera on a tripod on the beach in Rhodes by Grasser, Franz (Herstellung) (Fotograf) - Deutsche Fotothek, Germany - Public Domain

A Postcard From Every Corner of this Earth

During the era of the Grand Tour, souvenir shops everywhere had postcards. They were like a travelers’ own set of infinity stones, and many arranged them into collections for further study. The industrial revolution, an era when travel was made easier through railroads and steamships, was also the time photography was developed commercially. The railways made travel more accessible for everyone, and new ways of capturing the world through travel photography with portable cameras were abound.

  • !Image 11
  • !Image 12

Images: Postcard Early 20th Century Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons | Postcard of Piran early 20th cent_ Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons

Photographic souvenirs were a practical alternative if the English Brads and Chads couldn’t manage the equipment themselves. They were ready-made photos of key locations that influenced, and still do today, which locations were “important” enough to share. With new inventions, they could create their own photographs, and portable cameras such as the Kodak No. 1 and Folding Pocket Kodak changed the way these aristocratic fellows saw the world.

Image: Kodak Folding Pocket N1 Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons

A Note on Coloniality

All of this being said, many European aristocrats left these places messier than they found them. While many back home would respect their accounts as gentlemens’ guides to ancient history, in many ways, the Grand Tour served as an extension of imperial domination and Eurocentricism. Without getting too much into it, it is important to note that much of what we learn from this era is based on romanticized, and often appropriated, narratives.

Photography is a means to re-interpret historical archives. By re-examining travel and colonial photographic archives, we can critically view this time and re-center narratives that have been erased. As always, photography is a powerful artistic tool that can change how we think about history.

An Outro to this Escapade

I encourage you to go out into the world inspired by the passion to discover and learn about those who walk in different shoes. What unites us at Lomography, and in life, should be our desire to view things through a fresh lens, and while we work with the grain (of film), we should encourage one another in our differences just as much as in our similarities.

In the words of the late Anthony Bourdain, an inspiration to this writer:

> “If I’m an advocate for anything, it’s to move. As far as you can, as much as you can. Across the ocean, or simply across the river. The extent to which you can walk in someone else’s shoes or at least eat their food, it’s a plus for everybody. Open your mind, get up off the couch, move.”

Check out our Travel Guides for a Lomographic take on Travel, and as always, continue to share your creations with the Community.

Be sure to browse our cameras such as the Lomomatic 110 and Lomo’Instant lineup for a perfect portable postcard on your next trip. Finally, get inspired by the frames of our Analogue Archive to recreate some historical photos with a Lomographic look.

https://www.lomography.com/magazine/3588.content:
Seattle-based collage artist and illustrator Brian Hippern creates vibrant, hand-cut compositions inspired by nature, found materials, and the quiet moments of everyday life. Working with colored pencil drawings, vintage paper, handwritten letters, and carefully collected ephemera, his intuitive process balances thoughtful composition with spontaneity, allowing each piece to evolve organically.

For this edition of A Day With, we asked Brian to document a weekend in his creative life, from neighborhood coffee stops and treasure hunting for collage materials to long hours at the craft table bringing new works to life. Armed with the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass, he captured the people, places, and rituals that shape his artistic practice.

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Hello! Lomography asked me to document my creative process for the weekend using their instant camera. It went a little something like this:

> A rare weekend off in my life starts with a trip to get some coffee with my wife. We’re spoiled in Seattle to be surrounded by a seemingly endless amount of quality coffee shops. Today we went to Red Arrow Coffee, a neighborhood favorite with a plant covered terrace situation that hides away from the main street. It’s like a little oasis.

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> After coffee, I hit up the local art store, Push/Pull, for some extra paper. I go through a lot of paper making collage, so having an art store a few blocks away has been a massive benefit. I’m frequently after black mixed media paper, which usually functions as the base layer of all my collages. That stuff is like gold to me. I’m always on the hunt for black mixed media paper.

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> A quick trip across the street to the vintage books store, Ballard Books, was made to sift through their incredible selection for some collage source material. I have my own rules about sourcing, and try to focus on material that seems rejected, and offer it new life. Here, I found some handwritten letters from the early 1930s to use. I love used book store, estate sales and vintage shops for collecting collage material and especially love handwritten notes or letters.

> That is always a white whale for me: a letter written with good handwriting in black ink on old, good quality paper. Pure gold. I found an author’s prose writing rough drafts in a Life magazine from the 1960s at an estate sale once, that gave me a ton of mileage for collages. Something about a handwritten note carries some sort of mystic power with it. Not always, but I try to notice the ones that do. Do I sound crazy yet?

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> After the book store, it was time to get to work. My collages lately have been made up of my own colored pencil drawings, cut and arranged with layers of paper and accent notes of found collage material. So, the first step: draw something. It was a nice day, so I took my dog outside to the backyard picnic table with my sketchbook and pencils, and got to drawing.

> Lately, I’m focused on organic shapes, inspired by plant growth, the PNW, the yin and yang and playing with dimension. I try not to think too far ahead at this stage, and just freestyle. I know the general gist of what I’ll draw, but I let the rest just flow. Sometimes, I get too in my own head about making the perfect thing, when the best thing to do is just to listen to some music, and get lost in the drawing without having destination in mind.

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> The next day, I took to the craft table to cut up my drawings and start working on collaging. I have a huge amount of scrap paper in various colors. I like using various types of paper, it gives the collage some dimension, maybe not visible through a screen, but certainly in person. My secret weapon is washi paper, but I need to keep the brand a secret. I don’t want to gatekeep, but this brand of washi paper is perfect and always sold out. Sorry!

  • !Image 6
  • !Image 7

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Assembling the collages can take a while. There’s a little more planning involved than the drawing, but I try to keep things loose, and never be stubborn. These things are all about composition, so exploring different orientations or options that you didn’t think would work can sometimes unlock better avenues to go down. You have to know that you don’t know everything, you know?

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> I have a few showings coming up, so this month is really go-time in terms of production. I need to make a lot of work, especially because a lot of the time these collages aren’t great. I just make a bunch, try to work out the creative muscle, and trust that if I make enough, they’ll be some good ones from time to time.

Photo by Brian Hippern | Shot on the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Thank you to Lomography for giving me the opportunity to document my creative process, and to you, if you’re reading this, go buy a camera, silly! Pce n luv -hipski

Thank you Brian for documenting your artistic day for us! Make sure to check out his work on Instagram.

What's it like to be a film shutterbug living in some of the most well-known, iconic cities in the world? Our new series explores these cities through the eyes of local Lomographers, who share emerging, classic, and underrated art, music, food and historical spots, for anyone looking to immerse themselves in the soul of the sprawling metropolis.

We now have over 100 (and counting...) Travel Guides on our website, full of photography and travel inspiration tips around the globe. This time, we thought that we would let Lomographers themselves give us all the pieces we needed to create a Travel Guide for the romantically-ancient city of Rome.

  • !Image 1[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542604)
  • !Image 2[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/corinthian/photos/25009907)
  • !Image 3[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542742)
  • !Image 4[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/corinthian/photos/25009906)

Credits: johbeil&corinthian

Benvenuti a tutti to Rome, a city with a country inside its borders (yes, you read that right), the home of the first-ever shopping mall and a place where stray cats call the Colosseum home. A place full of history, where Gladiator sweat was once used as skincare and going to the toilets was a social activity. Oh, and don't forget about the nearly three-millennia-old Roman ruins you can discover, all with a film camera.

Let's dive into this city where you can walk the steps of warriors and enjoy a creamy carbonara on the same day, with the help of Lomographers Ugo Leonetti (@corinthian) and Johannes Beilharz (@johbeil). We reached out to them after finding their LomoHomes in our global Community. We sent over a list of questions and asked for their recommendations for the city they call home.

  • !Image 5[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/corinthian/photos/24789647)
  • !Image 6[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/25806864)

Credits: corinthian&johbeil

Hi, Ugo and Johannes, welcome to Lomography Magazine. Where do you currently reside, and how did you start taking film photography?

Ugo: I live in Quadraro, a working-class neighborhood in the southeast of the capital. I’ve been shooting on film since 2017, when my father gave me his Nikon FM after I had gone quite a while without taking photographs. It was also a period in my life when I needed to slow down and rethink things. Film photography became a kind of zen experience for me: it taught me once again the pleasure of looking at the world through a pentaprism and, above all, the value of cultivating patience and practice.

Johannes: I currently reside in Rome, Italy. My first encounter with film photography dates back to the early 1970s, when this was the only type of photography available. I still have photos and negatives from trips and other occasions from those days. With the advent of digital photography, I stopped taking photos on film for several years until 2015, when I took my father’s old Leicas out of their boxes and started using them again, thinking they were too good to remain unused. Since then, I’ve added many more film cameras, including medium format and pocket cameras.

  • !Image 7
  • !Image 8

Credits: corinthian – Tangenziale Est, Via Prenestina

What is it like becoming a film photographer in your city? Would you say there’s a strong film culture?

Ugo: Rome has a vibrant cultural spirit, shaped by the many influences and communities that come together there from across Italy and around the world. It is also, I would say, one of the most photographed cities in the world, so it's not uncommon to see someone carrying a small film camera around their neck, especially in the more “hipster” neighborhoods.

For instance, Rome is home to the main headquarters of Ars Imago, a shop specializing in analogue photography, and it's an easy place to meet fellow enthusiasts and strike up a conversation. There are also many venues that offer darkroom facilities, as well as courses in film developing and printing. I, for example, learned how to develop film in the basement of a Sapienza university social center that made its darkroom and equipment available to anyone interested in learning and practicing the craft.

Johannes: There is a film culture, as witnessed by some shows I’ve been to in different parts of the city. The lab in Torrino, where I have my films developed, does a substantial amount of analogue photo work. There is another thriving photo shop in Montagnola which sells and repairs mainly analogue cameras and offers film development.

  • !Image 9[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542601)
  • !Image 10[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542635)

Credits: johbeil

What’s your gear like? Are there any cameras or film stocks that stand out to you, especially in relation to photographing your city?

Ugo: The main thing is to travel light. I like to carry just one SLR and, at most, a point-and-shoot. Usually that means the aforementioned Nikon FM, a Pentax ME Super, or a Nikon FE, which has recently joined my collection thanks to an uncle who gifted it to me ;) along with an Olympus XA2.

In the past, if I was heading out to take photos, it wasn't unusual for me to bring two 35 mm camera bodies, a medium format camera, and a compact camera as well. Over time, though, I've realized that I prefer traveling light and focusing more on photography itself rather than on the gear.

As for film stocks, I think I've gone through miles of Fuji 200, Kodak ColorPlus, and Cinestill 800. I'm also very fond of motion-picture film stocks and films that produce distinctive effects, such as Lomography's LomoChrome Metropolis and LomoChrome Purple.

  • !Image 11
  • !Image 12

Credits: corinthian – Piazza di Porta and Rione Esquilino

Johannes: My main cameras are Leicas from the 1940s, 1950s, 1970s and 1980s and a variety of Olympus models dating from the 1960s to the 1980s. In addition to that, I have various Lomography cameras, e.g. Diana F+, Diana Mini, Sprocket Rocket, Fisheye, and cameras from other brands, e.g. Rollei, Seagull, Adox, Lubitel, Pentax, Voigtländer and Agfa.

Apart from mainstream films from Kodak, Fuji, Foma, Agfa and Ilford, I love experimental and unusual films like Adox Color Implosion, LomoChrome Purple and LomoChrome Turquoise, Lomography Redscale XR, Harman Red, Harman Azure. In the past, I also used slide films, mostly for cross-processing, which have unfortunately largely disappeared from the market or have become ridiculously expensive. I occasionally try my luck with expired films.

  • !Image 13[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542746)
  • !Image 14[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542699)

Credits: johbeil

Where do you usually hang out? Could you share favorite spots which might be considered underrated?

Ugo: I love Pigneto for the hectic and colorful lifestyle that somehow managed to remain authentic, same for Piazza Vittorio, that is considered the multicultural “Chinatown” of Rome.

Johannes: My most common photography hunting ground is my (expanded) vicinity, which means Roma Laurentino, EUR, Ostiense, Testaccio, Garbatella, Montagnola, San Paolo, all in the south of Rome. Of course, I also venture to the center and other parts of the city occasionally, e.g. Trastevere, the Jewish Quarter, the area around the Colosseum, Piazza Navona, to name just a few. And I love to explore other towns and places in Lazio, Abruzzo, Umbria, Molise, Puglia and their landscapes.

  • !Image 15[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542599)
  • !Image 16[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542600)

Credits: johbeil

What is your favorite photo walk route in your city?

Ugo: When I'm out of ideas, the route between San Lorenzo, Esquilino, Piazza Vittorio is a go-to and never disappoints you if you are willing to take some street photos.

Johannes: Most often I walk the “literary” streets of my vicinity – they are all named after writers, e.g. Marinetti, Silone, Pavese, Kafka, García Lorca, Melville, Baudelaire, Joyce, Woolf. Earlier this year, I published a book with some black and white photos taken in these streets. Contrary to the names, these streets are partially far from grand but run-down and therefore not very picturesque, but lend themselves to documentary or street photography. The crumbling brutalist architecture is also of some social significance.

Credits: corinthian – Devotional Wall, Largo Preneste

Have you taken any photos of your city that you consider your favorite? What’s the story behind it?

Ugo: Any pictures of forgotten and distant suburbs. I've managed to find something interesting and hypnotic in the ordinary, and somehow commonly considered ugly places I would never imagined to find something poetic in it.

Johannes: Some of my favorites are actually photos of more or less mundane motifs in the neighborhood or other parts. I’ve walked the same streets for years now but still occasionally manage to discover interesting details to photograph that I hadn’t noticed before. In some cases, expired films, camera or operator misbehavior have produced surprisingly interesting results.

[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/johbeil/photos/29542610)

Credits: johbeil

A Call to Our Community

We are constantly expanding our Travel Guides and would love your help. Just like with Ugo and Johannes in Rome, we want to hear your perspective, tips and tricks for the city you call home. If you feel like a city is missing, reach out to us at travel@lomography.com. We can't wait to hear from you!

UK-based director, photographer and videographer Joel Byron set out to capture a gig in his home town of Brighton by Reggae duo, The Tribulizations. He took along the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens, and let the looseness and personality of the lens capture the mood of the event. Joel talked to us about his experiences working with this unique bokeh lens and how letting go of your creative control can lead to some unexpected results.

Video 1

Welcome to the Magazine, Joel! Could you give us a quick introduction?

I’m a filmmaker and photographer based in Brighton, working through my studio BigPlus. Most of what I make sits somewhere between documentary and something more constructed. I’m not that interested in clean coverage. I’m more drawn to how something actually feels when you’re inside it. I move between digital and analogue depending on the project.

Film has always been a constant within my work, particularly Super 8 mm. I’m drawn to the texture, unpredictability and physicality of the format, and often collaborate with musicians and artists where those qualities become part of the final piece itself. I’ve been working closely with Reggae duo The Tribulizations, building a body of work around their night Moon-Hop at Komedia. It’s a good space for me. There’s rhythm, repetition, and a certain looseness that suits the way I like to shoot. Recently, I’ve been collaborating closely with them, documenting their new live night; Moon-Hop at Brighton’s Komedia and creating a Super 8 mm music video for their latest single, WON’T STOP!

Stills from The Tribulizations Live at Moon-Hop by Joel Byron | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Tell us about your time with the lens. Where did you take it and what did you end up shooting?

I took it straight to one of their nights and shot across the full run of the event. It doesn’t start until late, so most of it was captured between 11 pm and early morning. I kept the approach simple – moving between the stage, the edges of the room, and the crowd.

“Flare creeps in, edges soften, contrast shifts depending on how the light hits the lens. It feels less like a tool for recording and more like something that interprets what’s in front of it.”

At one point, I was shooting past the DJ booth as the lights cut from red into a cold white burst, and everything briefly flattened before dropping back into color again. Those shifts became the structure. It felt like the right environment because nothing holds still. You’re reacting all the time.

Stills from The Tribulizations Live at Moon-Hop by Joel Byron | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

What were your first impressions? How would you describe its personality?

It has a presence to it. You’re aware of it in your hand, and that changes how you shoot. It’s not interested in being neutral. It pushes the image in certain directions. Flare creeps in, edges soften, contrast shifts depending on how the light hits the lens. It feels less like a tool for recording and more like something that interprets what’s in front of it. You have to accept that fairly quickly or you end up fighting it.

Stills from The Tribulizations Live at Moon-Hop by Joel Byron | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Were there any particular moments – certain lighting setups or subjects – where the lens really came alive for you?

When the stage lights caught the front element at an angle, especially through smoke, it started to break the image apart in a really interesting way. I love the opening shot with the Komedia sign and also some of the MC, as he is framed with interesting light throws. There was a moment where the MC stepped forward into a wash of magenta and green, and instead of resolving cleanly, the light wrapped and bled across the frame. His outline held, but everything else shifted. That felt like the lens doing its best work. It responds to light hitting it imperfectly.

Stills from The Tribulizations Live at Moon-Hop by Joel Byron | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

How did the bokeh character influence the mood or style of your shots?

It pulled the background away from being descriptive and turned it into movement and color. I wasn’t trying to isolate subjects cleanly. I wanted things to drift. People moving through the frame, lights breaking up behind them, details appearing and then dissolving again. The bokeh helped with that. It gave the images a kind of rhythm rather than a fixed point. It felt closer to how the night actually reads when you’re there.

Stills from The Tribulizations Live at Moon-Hop by Joel Byron | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Any tips you’d share with someone curious to try this lens?

Don’t over-correct it. If you try to make everything sharp and controlled, you’ll lose what makes it interesting. Let the flare happen. Let things fall slightly out. Also, put it somewhere with contrast and movement. Mixed lighting, smoke, people crossing in and out of frame. It needs something to react to. If you treat it like a standard lens, you’ll probably miss what makes it interesting.

I’m currently working on a year long orchard project, documenting the cycle from blossom through to harvest using a mix of 16 mm, Super 8 mm and digital. I’d love to return to this lens in daylight and see how it responds in a completely different environment.

To see more of Joel's' work, visit the Big Studio Instagram page.

UK-based hobbyist Albert Cornelissen is curious about photography and the machines that help make the magic. When he's not testing out a new film or designing his own film camera, he likes to explore the beautiful UK countryside. When he received the new Lomo MC-A camera, he chose to break it in with a hike around the Peak District, a national park in England, with some Black & White 400 ISO film pushed to 800 ISO. We talked to Albert about his first impressions of this versatile new 35 mm camera.

  • !Image 1
  • !Image 2

Photos by Albert Cornelissen on the Lomo MC-A

Welcome to the Magazine! Could you give us a quick introduction about yourself and what you do?

Thank you! I'm Albert, a hobbyist photographer that started with film in my teenage years, went digital, and then eventually found my way back to analogue photography. I always carry some kind of camera with me, as long as it shoots film.

I use multiple formats, from 4x5 down to 110, and I am fortunate enough to have owned enough cameras to have (mostly) settled on a couple of favorites for each format. I also design and build my own film cameras, as well as bits and pieces adjacent to analogue photography, so I can appreciate the effort and engineering that went into the Lomo MC-A!

  • !Image 3
  • !Image 4

Photos by Albert Cornelissen on the Lomo MC-A

Tell us about the day you spent with the camera – where did you take it, and what did you decide to shoot?

The first day I put a proper roll through, I carried the Lomo MC-A along with me on one of my favorite local hikes, in the Peak District, up on the moors. Conditions tend to be challenging, with ever changing light and landscapes, so it's a good test of how capable a camera is.

“In the last few years, we've seen quite a few new film cameras being released, but the Lomo MC-A was the first one I felt could meet my needs for an every day carry film camera. I bought it minutes after it was announced!”

On this day, we had some beautiful light with light cloud cover, painting the peaks with contrast. Which meant I shot mostly landscapes. The photos from that day were amazing and have made some beautiful prints. The MC-A performed admirably.

  • !Image 5
  • !Image 6
  • !Image 7
  • !Image 8

Photos by Albert Cornelissen on the Lomo MC-A

What was your first impression? How would you describe its character?

In the last few years, we've seen quite a few new film cameras being released, but the Lomo MC-A was the first one I felt could meet my needs for an every day carry film camera. I bought it minutes after it was announced! Auto-everything (but manual if you prefer), premium materials, legendary optics. First impressions were good. After a few rolls you find that it's a Lomo for sure, but in the best way possible. Get to know it, and it gives you exactly what you expect.

I've always been a fan of the unique character of the Minitar lens, which is one of the main reasons I bought an MC-A. I shoot mostly black and white (HP5+ pushed to 800 mostly) and the lens on the Lomo MC-A delivers that punchy, contrasty look I love. If you can't tell, it's one of my favorites for 35 mm.

  • !Image 9
  • !Image 10
  • !Image 11
  • !Image 12

Photos by Albert Cornelissen on the Lomo MC-A

When would you feel most drawn to using the Lomo MC-A?

I'll pop it into a bag when I go hiking, take a walk to the pub, or when I travel abroad. I tend to use the MC-A as a snapshot camera, when I see something I think will make a nice picture, I point, aim, and shoot. I mostly shoot land- and cityscapes, but will do some off the cuff stuff too. Part of the charm of this camera is that it does all of the heavy lifting for you, and you really don't know what the photos will look like until you see your negatives. There's that anticipation that makes it pretty special. And then most of the resulting photos are great!

  • !Image 13
  • !Image 14
  • !Image 15

Photos by Albert Cornelissen on the Lomo MC-A

Any tips or thoughts you'd share with someone curious to try this camera for themselves?

Put in in auto and just burn through a roll or three. It really is that good. Yes, it has it quirks, but what most people don't realize is that bringing a new film camera this good to market is a feat in itself. With that in mind, you get to know this amazing little camera, you get past the quirks, and then you start playing with the more advanced features, and you realize what Lomography has done here. It's not perfect, but it's pretty close (for me at least).

  • !Image 16
  • !Image 17

Photos by Albert Cornelissen on the Lomo MC-A

To see more of Albert's work, visit his Instagram page and website.
