How much can we discover about someone through a handful of tiny questions? In this series, we’re exploring that very idea. With the tiny Lomomatic 110 in hand, we’re capturing the personalities, routines, and little moments that make someone who they are. Not long backstories, but honest answers, everyday rituals, and the unexpected details that reveal a life.

This time, we sat down with Aimee France for a very Aimee edition of Tiny Questions. Whether it's a three-drink minimum at breakfast or baking cakes that look like they've come straight out of a storybook, Aimee is known for her love of food, baking, and finding beauty in the quirky details of the everyday.

We get into the tiny questions that make you pause and romanticize summer, from the rituals and routines to the little moments that make the season feel special. From berry-picking plans to beach days and nostalgic summer soundtracks, these Tiny Questions offer a glimpse into the world through Aimee's eyes.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

Have you shot film before?

No. Only if my friends asks me to take photos on their cameras, and I need heavy instruction.

What were your first impressions of shooting 110 film?

I was confused by the setup initially. I needed a manual or a YouTube video. It's such a unique camera! Like how does the film even fit in the camera? My first photo was in front of Carmelo's, and I had to take it like seven times. It was so funny.

What surprised you about shooting with the Lomomatic 110?

How people thought it was so cool that I was using a film camera.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

Favorite thing about shooting with film for the past few weeks?

I take so many pictures every day on my phone, but there's something so special about taking out a camera. You know how people say “stop and smell the roses?” It's like that. You slow down for a second and live in the moment. You actually remember the photo you took. We take so many pictures on our phones. Looking through the film was so fun because I was like, “Oh my God, I actually remember trying to take that!”

Most “Aimee” photo you got back?

Maybe the one on the table with the two drinks, or the beach one. I really like that beach one.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

Favorite film?

LomoChrome Purple! I was telling all my friends it looked like I had a 2014 filter on my photos.

One place you want to bring the Lomomatic next?

I think when I go visit my parents. Just New England in the summer. I want to document the berry picking.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

What is the Aimee official coffee drink of the summer?

In the morning, a hot Americano. I need hot coffee no matter what. Later in the day, a coconut water coffee slushie! Frozen coconut water with chilled espresso.

Current three-drink minimum lineup?

Hot Americano with honey, green juice, kefir watered down with frozen blueberries and bee pollen, and hot citrus chia seed water with yuzu juice and Celtic salt. Kind of Nature's Gatorade.

Why do you think breakfast requires a multi-drink balance?

I think I wake up dehydrated, and I like a lot of different flavors. The way people pair alcohol with food, I like pairing drinks with breakfast.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

What's one thing you're saying yes to this summer?

Any plans. If someone invites me to something, there's a 98% chance I'll go. I'm in it for the bit. I had an epiphany this summer that I haven't really lived life in the past five years. I used to have a business making cakes, and when you're a self-employed baker, your life revolves around the process. It feels amazing to have a social life again and have the energy for new connections.

What's one thing you're trying to get better at this summer?

Working on my social skills. Being more open to meeting whoever and hanging with new people. It takes practice. I don't think I'm bad at socializing, but it's good not to always surround yourself with the same people. You have to push your comfort zone.

Right now: party girl era or calm, routine queen?

I'm going out a lot, but I still have my routine. I'm allowing myself some grace. I still have to do my routine, but I've been letting myself do things a little more relaxed.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

What's your summer uniform?

I've really been liking a mini skirt or shorts with either a polo or a button-up with a nice shoulder. Or just slipping on a dress, something chill and light. Orthopedic flip-flops, Oofos. I'm putting miles on those!

What are three must-have items in your bag for the summer?

A lot of lip products – like, way too many. It's ridiculous. I have over 25. Other than that? Maybe a compact mirror, gum, and either hand sanitizer or headphones. Probably hand sanitizer.

Song of the summer?

For some reason, and I've thought this for so long, Katy Perry is summer. When you go back and listen in May, June, and July, it just hits so different. One of the Boys and Teenage Dream. I'm immediately back in elementary school, and it's officially summer break.

Who inspired you to bake and cook?

Probably my deepest root is my mom. She used to make me a birthday cake every year, one year it was a Wacky Zingoz cake. I would watch her make this chocolate cake using a recipe from a bakery she worked at. It was my favorite cake. I have this vivid memory of the stand mixer being so scary. I taught myself eventually, and now I'm no longer scared of a stand mixer.

In this moment: jammy egg or scrambled egg?

Scrambled egg. Kind of crazy, I know. But the jammy egg will come back.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

What summer produce are you most interested in this year?

I've been eating a lot of Little Gem lettuce, but that's more early summer. Stone fruit. More snacking vegetables to dip in hummus because it's so hot I don't want to cook. And tarragon for an herb.

First booth you're hitting at the farmers market?

In the summer, somewhere with berries or tomatoes. But I always do a full loop before making any decisions. The hottest commodity I found recently was a farm selling salmon raspberries. I stopped dead in my tracks, and I just had to get them.

Favorite farmers market in the city?

Union Square. Recently I've also been loving the Maria Hernandez market. They've really stepped up their game this year.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

Favorite PB&J combo currently?

Well, when I've been making the Uncrustable videos, I usually have a nut butter and jam I want to highlight. But by the end, when I'm meal prepping and just making them for myself, I throw whatever I have together: Ground Up nut butter, the coconut almond cashew butter, my homemade pistachio butter, and blueberry chia seed jam. That combo? It was nuts.

What makes Uncrustables so perfect?

A peanut butter and jelly is just so nostalgic, and an Uncrustable is so nostalgic. My friend Paige loves Uncrustables, and one time we went on a suburban target run and she got them. The ingredients kind of freaked me out, so I wanted to make my own. So I got the little press and started making them. They're such an amazing summer lunch. I love a little kid's lunch. I'm just really passionate about it.

What's your late-night bodega order?

Usually, we're having dinner and then going out. So by the time I get home I'm falling asleep. So honestly? Coconut water. A cup of ice. Or North Dumpling.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

Favorite summer movie?

I've been randomly going to the movies with friends lately. Eric Rohmer's films have been feeling really romantic and summery. Pauline at the Beach.

Team Edward or Team Jacob?

Team Edward. He's just so hot and toxic.

Favorite Twilight film?

All of them. But nothing compares to the first one.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

Stripes or polka dots?

Stripes.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

Laying horizontal in the park or on the beach?

Beach.

Beach picnic or backyard Ridgewood BBQ?

Beach picnic. One hundred percent.

Favorite beach for a picnic with friends?

I went to a really nice beach in Jersey. I couldn't tell you where it was – I just get driven to Jersey and I don't ask questions. Jacob Riis is always great too.

Photo by Aimee France | Shot with the Lomomatic 110 on Color Tiger 110

You've been branching out into new content. Are you feeling fulfilled?

Yes and no. I still feel a little intimidated by it. I feel like my audience doesn't want to see it, but that could just be in my head. You put yourself in a bubble, and it might just be a me thing. I know I can always post food content.

Anything coming up soon our readers should look out for?

I'm making a sandwich collaboration with Edith's in September – a sandwich and a slushie. Flavor TBD. Also, if anyone wants someone for modeling...I've been doing more of that lately and would love to do more.

Thanks, Aimee, for answering our Tiny Questions! Make sure to check her out on Instagram!

Summer has a way of making even the smallest moments feel worth remembering: backyard pool parties, melting popsicles, sun-soaked afternoons, and friends who somehow turn every gathering into a photoshoot. Lucky for us, photographer Cassie McCoy ([](https://www.instagram.com/churbumgirl/)@churbumgirl) had the new Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor for exactly that kind of day.

Known for her emotionally rich portraits and playful approach to analogue photography, Cassie's latest series leans into the carefree side of summer without losing the thoughtful storytelling that defines her work. We caught up with her to chat about finding joy in simplicity, embracing the unexpected magic of half-frame photography, and why sometimes the best images happen when you stop chasing perfection.

  • !Image 1
  • !Image 2
  • !Image 3
  • !Image 4

Photos by Cassie McCoy | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Hey, Cassie, welcome back to Lomography Magazine! It's been a while since we last caught up. For readers who may not be familiar with your work, can you tell us how you first got into analogue photography, and what makes the medium so important to your creative practice?

Always a pleasure to be back!

I got my first point-and-shoot film camera, which was partly broken, when I was 18 at a thrift store in rural Ohio for six bucks. My introduction to film set the course for a scrappy style that eventually solidified into intense storytelling through portraits. My process will always retain its frugal roots, thanks to my dad, who was raised in a working-class mill town in southern Ohio. Work with what you have is my mantra at this point, which is also a great principle to follow when you're starting out in any artistic medium.

I stay loyal to film, of course, for its look, but also because the process forces you to be in your body. Whether I'm taking fun, spontaneous shots on the street or working one-on-one with a model, carefully considering how the light hits their face to tell the vision we've built together, I'm never thinking about what's behind me or the endless scroll of my to-do list. I hear my breath. I feel the buttons beneath my fingers. I hear the shutter and feel it shake through me. I'm not scared. My eyes go wide, and I take everything in.

Did you have previous experience with the half-frame format? What was your first impression of the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Camera?

Yes! I actually used my LC-Wide's half-frame setting for some self-portraits during the winter. My childhood home's basement was being demolished and renovated, and I thought it would be cool to shoot photos within all the mess and rebuilding.

It was interesting to see how the LC-Wide's half-frame images blurred together, but I ended up really liking the stark dividing line of the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera even more. It makes me want to scribble all over the frames with my writing and see the photos laid out in a book or zine.

Photos by Cassie McCoy | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Tell us about your experience with the camera. Where did you go and what did you shoot? We're sad we didn't get the invite to the Midwest pool party!

You're always welcome to a backyard bash in the Midwest! I went up to my friend Sarah's place in Cleveland with my best friend, Lex. Sarah and Lex have known each other for years and know how to turn even a cool-down into a catwalk. We soaked up the sun while Sarah set up her shark pool, played mermaids, got sprayed by the hose, and enjoyed popsicles and cherries, naturally.

Your work often explores themes of femininity, identity, and perception, but this roll feels especially playful and carefree. What inspired you to take the camera in that direction?

My recent work with portraits has taken a more serious, emotionally heavy direction that has been centered around me and my growing pains. I live a life full of constant change fueled by a drive to evolve. My friend recently compared me to Darwin’s Galapagos finches, if that helps to paint a picture. As I've grown as an artist and now being a 23-year-old woman, I’ve realized that my need to play and let loose with others is something I never want to say goodbye to; my style was built by taking my cameras to parties and concerts in college with my girls, and it's a nice feeling to know that I can tap back into that joyous yet impish energy whenever I want/need to.

I needed a day to let my inner girl run around in the summer sun, splash with her friends, and to soak in the sweetness the unconditional love of creativity and connection gives me.

  • !Image 6
  • !Image 7

Photos by Cassie McCoy | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

The Half-Frame Simple Use Camera is a reloadable camera with built-in flash and interchangeable color gel filters, and true to its name, simple to use. Which of its features did you enjoy the most, or pushed you creatively into different directions?

You already know I was all over the built-in flash. Flash is an essential part of my process, no matter the time of day or location. Daylight flash can elevate a scene like nothing else. In addition to my addiction to brightness, I always get some great reactions from friends and strangers because my flash is always on.

Is there a specific photo from this roll that stood out to you or left a lasting impression? What's the story behind it?

The photo of my best friend Lex in her sunglasses next to the photo of the bright blue sky resonated with me so much. She's been through so much with me, not only as a friend but as a creative. Our very first hangout was actually a photoshoot I did of her!

This photo feels emotional because of our connection, but also because of its freshness. It's just so simple and real. It reflects the direction my style started taking this past winter, especially when I began using borders to give my work a little room to breathe.

Photo by Cassie McCoy | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Around that time, I started making mock-up zines using Lomography Color Negative '92 Sun-Kissed alongside messy typography pulled from my journals, inspired by David Carson, a personal hero of mine. Those photo spreads finally combined elements I'd been wanting to bring together for years, and they also helped me process a difficult period in my life. They were never meant for anyone else, just for me to process and to express gratitude for the things in my life that kept me stable.

Photo by Cassie McCoy | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Was there a song playing in your head while shooting the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera? If you could describe your experience with the camera through a song, what song would that be?

Yes! Angel in L.A. by Kelli Ali, the voice of the cult-classic triphop group Sneaker Pimps.

Trip hop captures so many different essences at once: unconventionality, sensuality, seriousness, boldness, and playfulness. Those are feelings I hope come through in any medium I work in. Angel in L.A. is equipped with a multitude of instruments in its production that strays away from structure, yet the unexpected turns keep you engaged and excited.

Kelli's fresh, flirty presence could make anyone starstruck, inviting them to have a little fun and to enjoy the dance of life. We leaned into the playful, brighter side of triphop at our pool party, still packed with the vividness that life and art has to offer.

Your work often embraces imperfection, whether through experimental film stocks, unexpected color shifts, or fleeting moments. Did the simplicity of this camera encourage you to let go of control and trust the process in a different way?

Absolutely. Anything I can do to simplify my process, and my life, is something I welcome now. Film can become an overcomplicated medium where people worry about every frame and chase perfection, but that should never be your first thought. In many ways, that mirrors the feminine experience that shows up in my process: learning to move beyond those expectations of perfection, whether they're from manmade molds or marked by our mothers.

  • !Image 10
  • !Image 11

Photos by Cassie McCoy | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Any tips for shooting the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera?

Invite variety! My favorite half-frame photos come from unexpected juxtapositions. Change your subject every frame, shoot from different angles, or mix close-ups with landscapes. The pairings often become even more interesting than the individual images.

Where else would you take the camera?

I'd love to see this camera in action at a rooftop DJ set just after sunset, during blue hour. The colored flash gels would make for some incredible scenes. Going back to Lisbon is always on my mind. I'd love to photograph the bustle of Feira da Ladra with my friends. The juxtapositions of all the different objects from the vendors, mixed with the constant flow of people and emotions, would be incredible.

I'd also take it on a bike ride with my boyfriend, @samrubin, and try capturing motion alongside Pittsburgh's bright yellow bridges. I promise to be careful!

Any parting words for our readers?

Take your camera everywhere, especially if you have a point-and-shoot! You never know what you'll stumble upon or who you'll run into on a grocery trip, and it's okay if you don't get the perfect shot. I've never felt burnt out by photography because I've tried to keep that mindset. When you stay lighthearted and curious, every roll will always feel like you're just starting out, and that is the best feeling in the world.

Photo by Cassie McCoy | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor

Thanks to Cassie for testing out the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera ! Make sure to check out more of her work on Instagram

https://www.lomography.com/magazine/3589.content:
Our Magazine series, Creators in Focus, highlights experimental minds around the world who are pushing boundaries, and finding new ways to live life more analogue.

What if there was an alternative photographic process which could truly be sustainable at its core? While film photography allows for a slower and controlled pace to material application, admittedly its heavy use of chemicals and water in developing leaves a substantial carbon footprint. This field of study is where Martha Gray’s BioCyan and adjunct experiments reside.

With research spanning more than a decade, Martha has pioneered a process which explores the potential of biomaterials as a photographic substrate. By fusing the non-toxic nature of cyanotypes with a medium composed of natural polymers, she reframes photographic notions of environmental degradation and image permanence through her works such as Technofossil (2025); Decomposition (2025); and most recently, Windows (2026). Through this interview, we had the opportunity to learn more about Martha and her biomaterial compositions.

Credits: Martha Gray | Process, cyanotype & SolarFast bioplastic prints, 2021 - 2025

Welcome to the Lomography Magazine Martha! Could you please tell us a little about yourself and what you do?

Hi, thank you for asking me to share about my work with the Lomography Community! I’m an artist and curator from London whose practice revolves around combining biomaterials and photography.

**We saw that your previous work in the BioCyan series depicted images shot with a 35 mm film camera. Prior to working on biotextiles, can you share with us when you

started doing analogue photography? What sparked your curiosity?**

I began taking analogue photos when I was 13, after I started a darkroom course because I was struggling in school and needed an outlet. I was interested in both art and sciences and immediately connected with analogue photography as it merged both without being tied to academic performance.

I was experimenting a lot with things like solarisation, multi exposures, hand coloring, as well as some abstract color work. I continued working with analogue photography for quite a few years until my medium changed to alternative processes. I still keep a 35 mm photo album though which is often the imagery I use in my bioplastic prints.

Credits: Martha Gray | Untitled, bioplastic cyanotype print, 2026

**Throughout the years, you’ve amassed quite the expansive research on biotextiles and alternative photographic processes! Could you walk us through your story to when it

all began, from working with cyanotype as your primary medium to the conception of infusing bioplastic technology?**

I started working primarily with cyanotype when the Darkroom at the place I was studying closed for half the year and I needed to make images without it. Cyanotype was something more versatile and tactile I could do from home and I felt more freedom to experiment with image making and discovered that my artistic style is process driven, not image driven.

Over time I became interested in the chemistry of cyanotype through chemigrams and the subsequent health and safety assessments of combining chemicals and organic materials. When the pandemic started I was in the first year of my MA in Art & Science at CSM and needed to be able to create from home which is when I first began working with biomaterials.

Credits: Martha Gray | Blueprint tryptic, bioplastic cyanotype print, 2022

Biomaterials & Alternative Analogue Photography Processes

For context, what are biotextiles? And how did you happen upon your research on combining biomaterials and alternative photography?

Biomaterials are materials created using organic sources like algae, eggshell, cornstarch, and SCOBY that fall into different categories depending on the materials behavior and ingredients used. A biomaterial can also be more than one thing, such as biotextiles can be bioplastics if they are made with agar which is a natural polymer.

Algae based bioyarn, for example, functions like string in its materiality, making it a biotextile, but is also made from the natural polymer of algae, making it also a bioplastic. Typically most recipes contain a biopolymer as a binder meaning they can all technically be bioplastics. Biotextiles are biomaterials that function as a textile. I tend to use the terms pretty interchangeably as I see my work as cross-disciplinary between the biomaterial definitions.

Credits: Martha Gray | (L) Untitled, woven bioyarn cyanotype print of hand, 2026 | (C) Folded Bioplastic Cyanotype | (R) Cyanotype biolplastic print Process/experiment - Underdeveloped bioplastic

My research started as part of a residency with the Sustainable Darkroom to look into sustainable darkroom processes but was disrupted by the first pandemic lockdown. Since I had cyanotype chemistry at home, I was curious to see if I could reduce chemical wash off into water systems through material applications. I began looking at glass cyanotypes due to the absorbent qualities of Gelatin but wanted a more sustainable alternative, which led me to agar and bioplastics. At that time, I could only find one post from someone using agar instead of gelatin when making glass cyanotypes, so I had to learn through experimentation.

“I prefer to never really know what kind of results I will get which is why I never make my work uniform, each piece is unique. Novelty in process and outcome and a love of learning through making is the driving force behind my practice...”

I did some research into bioplastics but mostly made up my own recipes and messed around with different ingredients, drying formats, exposures, surfaces, and so on. Initially I was placing the bioplastic cyanotype on paper, and then one day a piece dried and peeled itself off becoming an object. This is when I realized the potential for biomaterials as photographic substrates and essentially became obsessed with it, and still am.

Credits: Martha Gray | Technofossil, framed, bioplastic cyanotype print, 2025

At present we’ve seen that you’ve been experimenting with more photographic processes on biomaterials such as SolarFast, coffee-toned cyanotype, and underdeveloped bioplastic. Could you walk us through your experimentation process? How do you conceptualize your projects, and what materials or techniques do you consider/apply?

I’m never making work thinking about a finished artwork or image, it’s more so, ‘I wonder what would happen if I did this’ or ‘is it possible to do this’. Since bioplastics and photography are a newer medium, it leaves me plenty of space to experiment and discover with it always feeling new and exciting. I prefer to never really know what kind of results I will get which is why I never make my work uniform, each piece is unique. Novelty in process and outcome and a love of learning through making is the driving force behind my practice, I think.

“The only way to find out is to make it and put it out there and have whatever outcome become a part of the artwork.”

Previously I was very focused on getting my personal process perfected, and since biomaterials are not massively known, my work was responding to the desire to showcase that these were analogue and organic photographic objects. I wanted the images to be very sharp photographic prints and to see if the bioplastic could be treated like paper, so I was bleaching, toning, and trying out other processes like SolarFast.

Then as I became more confident in my process I delved into intentionally disrupting it, like allowing bubbles in the bioplastic, under developing the agar, allowing bioplastic to cool and congeal. As well as other things like placing them on objects such as vases and mirrors, and cutting them up to create my sculptural flower piece.

Credits: Marth Gray | (L) SolarFast biolplastic print | (CL) SolarFast biolplastic print

Process/experiment - Bubbles in bioplastic | (R) SolarFast biolplastic print

Now I’m moving into developing my original recipe to alter its materiality, playing around with making things of different sizes, textures, colors, and so on. I’m making a book with bioplastic being the page material, which is interesting as every page is interacting visually with one another due to its translucency. It's been quite a process of layering to create something that's compelling, as all the prior or following images are still visible once a page is turned.

The challenge from this will be, how does the material respond to being frequently touched? Will the oils from peoples skin, humidity from their breath, heat from their hands, alter it? Maybe. The only way to find out is to make it and put it out there and have whatever outcome become a part of the artwork. If I like it, then great. If I don’t, then I will figure out new ways and inform what I wish to create next.

Credits: Martha Gray | Windows, bioplastic, cyanotype, SolarFast, 2026

With around a decade of experience working with alternative photographic processes, what are some of your favorite experiments and projects?

That's a tough question! It feels hard to separate things into projects or experiments because it's been a continuous thread from one thing to the next with half of that time being my bioplastics and alternative processes research. I guess I’ve really enjoyed experimenting with photography more so as an object, and my time on my MA, as that was when I found my voice as an artist.

Credits: Martha Gray | Biocyan, installation shot, Art & Science MA Degree Show, Bioplastic cyanotype Print, 2021

English botanist and photographer Anna Atkins seems to play a prominent and recurring role in your work, could you expound on the ways she has influenced your process? Apart from her, are there other people you turn to for reference or inspiration?

Yes, my MA work was, in a way, a reimagining of Atkins’s who is known for documenting British algae species using cyanotype, resulting in her books titled Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions. Created in 1843 and believed to be the first book illustrated by photographs, Anna Atkins is a representation of how art and science was more intersectional at the time.

Credits: Martha Gray | Technofossil, bioplastic cyanotype print, 2025

Agar, which is the base for my bioplastic, is derived from algae, so there was this connection between my work and Atkins as both use cyanotype and algae to explore photography’s capabilities. This was early in my research with bioplastic, and early in bioplastic and photography as a process generally.

“Photography was created out of the Industrial Revolution which was the accelerator for capitalism, it's a medium that was developed with little consideration for environmental impact. I believe it's important to examine any desensitization we may have to this and reflect on our approaches to creating.”

So, it felt like I was discovering something new akin to Atkins as cyanotype was invented in 1842, making Atkins one the first people to ever use it. Also, as early women photographers have often been ignored from the historical record, it is influential to women artists like myself to have a figure like Atkins, even if we are still challenged in viewing Atkins through the canon in which she exists.

The other people I turn to for reference and inspiration are my peers, as there is strong community and dialogue within analogue and alternative processes. These mediums are so process-driven and experimental that we are constantly learning from one another.

Credits: Martha Gray | (L) Cyanotype & SolarFast biolplastic print Process/experiment - Layering of photographic processes | (R) Cyanotype biolplastic print Process/experiment - Bleached and coffee-toned cyanotype

Sustainability: Material Awareness & Conscious Consumption in Analogue Photography

Your latest projects ‘Decomposition’ and ‘Technofossil,’ both done in 2025, tackle issues on environmental degradation through plastic and other unsustainable human interventions. ‘Decomposition’ also highlights the unsustainable nature of Photography as a medium. Could you talk about the advocacy behind your creations, what ecological concerns you would like to highlight both within the photography industry and in general, as well as steps towards addressing such?

As my bioplastic work developed, I’ve been exploring what it means in a theoretical context to combine photography and plastics and how the relationship between photography and synthetic plastics has become materially entangled with the other over time. I’ve been reflecting on how much plastic we use in photography and I found the ethical implication of that a bit overwhelming.

For example, I have printed with resin-coated paper – resin can take thousands of years to break down, yet the paper with the image I created on it will be gone long before that. This personally feels like way too much responsibility. I don’t feel comfortable deciding if my art is so important that it should have that much of an impact on the Earth.

Credits: Martha Gray | (L) Decomposition micro photograph of snail eating bioplastic cyanotype print | (R) Decomposition micro photograph of millipede eating bioplastic cyanotype print

I had already been experimenting with the biodegradable nature of my bioplastic cyanotypes and this research brought it to the forefront. Cyanotype is non-toxic and has a lot of iron in it, which in combination with the food grade materials of non commercial bioplastics, makes for a highly biodegradable object.

While it is impossible to fully remove synthetic plastics from your life, I can create a plastic-free image which feeds the Earth instead of polluting it. Even if this means the destruction of my work, I can instead choose to incorporate that into the work and I see it as the life cycle of an image. Prior to this, I was focused on making the materials used in my process repurposable and free from disposable plastics to the best of my ability, as I strongly advocate for material awareness and conscious consumption.

Credits: Martha Gray | Technofossil, bioplastic cyanotype print, 2025

I also have an issue with the use of continuous running water in analogue and alternative photography if it's not a strict requirement. I only soak my works when washing and bioplastic as a substrate requires minimal photographic chemistry, allowing for reduced water usage.

Photography was created out of the Industrial Revolution which was the accelerator for capitalism, it's a medium that was developed with little consideration for environmental impact. I believe it's important to examine any desensitization we may have to this and reflect on our approaches to creating.

Credits: Martha Gray | (L) Cyanotype biolplastic print Process/experiment - Overexposed and bleached cyanotype | (C) Cyanotype biolplastic print Process/experiment - Scale (Large) | (R) Cyanotype biolplastic print Process/experiment - Early bioplastic cyanotype (Biocyan)

**Personally, what issues have you faced in your experimentation process? How did you address these, and are there any pieces of advice you could provide the Lomography

Community on alternative photographic processes?**

I would say the two main issues are safety and space. With analogue photography, you have dedicated spaces in darkrooms with safety regulations, whereas with alternative processes, often people are doing them at home or in studios.

While alternative photographic processes are safe to work with, there is always an inherent risk when working with chemistry. When you are working from a private space and being quite experimental like I am, you have to think about things like ventilation or chemical interactions.

Credits: Martha Gray | Untitled, SolarFast & bioplastic cyanotype print, 2026

Some modern processes do not list their ingredients so you don’t immediately know what you're working with. Older ones can contain potentially dangerous chemicals like cyanotype, which is safe and non-toxic in its formulation but does consist of Potassium Ferricyanide. This chemical cannot be heated to extreme temperatures or be exposed to high concentrations of acids as it could turn into cyanide. It is extremely unlikely that a person could create the conditions at home to produce this reaction but you should always be aware when working with chemistry.

When it comes to space, you often have to create your own as commercial darkrooms do not have facilities for alternative processes or things like film soup or natural developers. You get used to being pretty DIY with how you work and personally I enjoy the freedom of it, but it can definitely be a challenge. So, my advice would be to always be safe when working with chemistry and be creative with how you use your space.

Credits: Martha Gray | (L) Cyanotype biolplastic print Process/experiment - Coffee-toned cyanotype | (R) Cyanotype & SolarFast biolplastic print Process/experiment - Layering of photographic processes

**Apart from your personal projects, we also saw that you were a project leader for the London Alternative Photography Collective (LAPC). Could you expound on your role

within the organization, and events/exhibitions that you’ve enjoyed working on?**

As a Project Leader I am supported with developing any project ideas I have that I wish to pursue as part of the collective. Through 2024 and 2025, I lead on a collaboration between LAPC and the Linnean Society of London which is the oldest active society devoted to natural history. I developed a program to accompany the Linnean Society’s exhibition, Still Life: Depicting Nature from Woodcuts to X-Rays, which displayed scientific works from the early days of photography.

I ran cyanotype workshops using Linnean Society's botanical specimen collection for prints, and was lucky enough for their copy of Anna Atkins' book to be displayed as a part of the workshop. We also had talks by some amazing photographers such as Dianne Bos and Gem Toes-Crichton, whose work explores themes of natural history collections. This was a real passion project for me as someone whose art practice is centered around the intersection of art and science in both historical and contemporary contexts.

Credits: Martha Gray | Decomposition, Time lapse of bioplastic cyanotype print in home compost being broken down by soil organisms, 2025

Lastly, are there any ongoing or future projects that you’d like to share with the Lomography community?

Recently, I’ve been working as a part of the Alternative Processes team on a collaboration with the Photobook Cafe, as a co-curator of The Process Room. This project is a program of workshops, an exhibition celebrating the art of experimentation within alternative photographic processes, and photobooks through DIY methodologies and shared visual aesthetics. As I mentioned earlier, I’m currently working on a book and have a few other experiments in the works like creating woven images with bioyarn and cyanotype.

Credits: Martha Gray | Windows, bioplastic, cyanotype, SolarFast, 2026

Analogue endures through material processes, lived rhythms, and practices that ask us to slow down. Creators in Focus follows these sensibilities beyond photography, through voices like Martha's that keep analogue alive across disciplines.

We’d like to thank Martha for sharing her story and art with us! To see more of her work, you can visit her Instagram page and website.

When people think of Southern Thailand, destinations like Phuket, Krabi, Phang Nga, or Trang usually come to mind. As a result, places like Nakhon Si Thammarat are often overlooked. And if someone does mention Nakhon Si Thammarat, chances are they're talking about Ban Khiri Wong, the peaceful village surrounded by lush mountains that's often praised for having the cleanest air in Thailand.

For this trip, however, I decided to do something different. Instead of heading to the countryside, I spent my time exploring the heart of Nakhon Si Thammarat – known locally as Muang Khon. I wanted to discover what this historic city had to offer, and see where my very first solo trip would take me.

Let's get started!

Film: LomoChrome 35 mm Classicolor ISO 200

I've wanted to travel solo for a long time, and when a long holiday came around from May 30th to June 3rd, I finally decided to stop thinking about it and just go. The trip came together surprisingly last minute, which somehow made it even more exciting.

Originally, I planned to take the train from Bangkok to Nakhon Si Thammarat so I could spend the journey watching the scenery roll by. Unfortunately, because of the holiday, every train was fully booked. My backup plan was an overnight coach instead – which meant spending 12 hours on a bus. Let's just say...my back wasn't very happy.

Film: LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

I left Bangkok in the evening and arrived in Nakhon Si Thammarat around 6 a.m. the next morning, officially beginning my first solo adventure. Before heading anywhere, I loaded my first roll of film: LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200. Since the city is filled with charming historic buildings, I thought the film's classic color palette would suit the atmosphere perfectly.

Since check-in at my hostel wasn't until 2 p.m., I had plenty of time to explore the city. My first stop was Wat Phra Mahathat Woramahawihan, one of Nakhon Si Thammarat's most iconic landmarks.

Film: LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

As luck would have it, my visit coincided with Visakha Bucha Day, so the temple was filled with worshippers and visitors, creating an incredibly lively atmosphere.

Camera: Lomomatic 110 | Film: Color Tiger 110 ISO 200

Outside the temple, souvenir stalls lined the streets, and local artisans demonstrated how to make Khanom La, one of Southern Thailand's best-known traditional desserts.

Film: LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

I also was also lucky enough to visit during the season for Mangkhut Khat, a local snack made from peeled young green mangosteens. Chilled before serving, they were wonderfully crisp and refreshing in the nearly 40°C heat.

Camera & Film: (L) Lomomatic 110&Color Tiger 110 ISO 200 | (R) LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

My next destination was the Suchat Subsin Shadow Puppet Folk Museum, founded by Suchat Subsin, a National Artist recognized for his contributions to Thailand's traditional performing arts. The museum houses an impressive collection of Nang Talung (Southern Thai shadow puppets), including puppets over a century old, as well as examples from other regions of Thailand and even from around the world.

The galleries were fairly dimly lit, so I loaded a roll of Berlin Kino B&W ISO 400, pushing it two stops to ISO 1600. I have to admit, I was a little surprised when I got the negatives back. The grain was absolutely wild!

Film: Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400 (Pushed to 1600)

One of the museum's highlights was a live demonstration of how Nang Talung puppets are made – from preparing and drying cowhide, to carving the intricate patterns and painting each figure by hand. I even got to see freshly prepared hides drying outside, though unfortunately, I was too slow to grab a photo before moving on.

Film: Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400 (Pushed to 1600)

Before leaving, I couldn't resist taking one last photo of the museum's resident cat. It was far too adorable to pass up the opportunity.

Film: Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400 (Pushed to 1600)

After that, it was finally time to check into my hostel. The building itself was beautiful – it had originally served as a school before being thoughtfully converted into a hostel, preserving much of its original character and charm.

Film: LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

The following morning, before heading to another museum, I spotted something I don't usually see outside Southern Thailand, a Red-whiskered Bulbul in its cage. These birds are a common pet in the region, but this particular one was completely white, a much rarer color variation. It was too interesting to ignore, so I pulled out my Lomomatic 110 and snapped a quick photo.

Camera: Lomomatic 110 | Film: Color Tiger 110 ISO 200

My next stop was the National Museum of Nakhon Si Thammarat, which houses archaeological discoveries from four southern provinces: Chumphon, Surat Thani, Nakhon Si Thammarat, and Phatthalung. The collection spans everything from prehistoric artifacts and Buddhist relics to objects connected with Hinduism, ancient ceramics, and many other historical treasures.

Film: Kodak Vision3 250D

Photographing inside the museum proved to be quite challenging. I was shooting on Kodak Vision3 250D, which meant working with relatively slow shutter speeds under the dim gallery lighting. As a result, I had to be selective with every frame and came away with fewer photographs than I'd hoped, but that's all part of shooting film.

Film: Kodak Vision3 250D

After leaving the museum, I hopped onto one of the city's Songthaews (shared pickup trucks that serve as local public transport) to explore more of Muang Khon. I got off near the City Pillar Shrine and wandered around the neighborhood for a while.

Film: Kodak Vision3 250D

I made sure to do most of my sightseeing in the morning, as it had become clear that rain arrived almost every afternoon during my stay, often continuing into the evening.

Film: LomoChrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

The following day was my last full day of sightseeing. I only had two places left on my list: the Old City Wall and the Nakhon Si Thammarat City Museum. Since I knew I'd be photographing historic architecture for most of the day, I decided to load an expired roll of Berlin Kino B&W ISO 400. I thought its vintage look would pair perfectly with the centuries-old city walls.

Film: Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400

After photographing the Old City Wall, I headed to the Nakhon Si Thammarat City Museum. The museum walks visitors through the city's history from the Sukhothai period to the Rattanakosin era, while also exploring the arrival and development of Buddhism and other religious influences in the region. Rather than focusing on archaeological artifacts, the exhibitions rely on information panels, videos, and life-size dioramas to tell the story of the city.

Film: Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400

Although it doesn't house as many historical objects as the National Museum, it offers a much broader understanding of Nakhon Si Thammarat's past and helped me appreciate how important the city has been throughout Thai history.

Film: Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400

The museum building itself is also a fantastic subject for black-and-white photography. If you enjoy photographing architecture on film, this is definitely a place worth bringing your camera to.

Film: Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400

I still had two more days left in Nakhon Si Thammarat after finishing my sightseeing itinerary, but by then I'd already visited every place I wanted to see. So instead of chasing more landmarks, I simply slowed down – wandering through the streets, trying local food, stopping wherever looked interesting, and letting the city set the pace.

Unfortunately, by that point I'd run out of film, so I don't have any more photographs to share.

Although Nakhon Si Thammarat isn't usually the first destination people think of when planning a trip to Southern Thailand, spending a few days here completely changed my perspective. It's a city where history, religion, and diverse cultural influences blend together naturally. Life moves at a gentler pace, the old town is full of character, public transportation makes getting around surprisingly easy, and the air somehow feels fresher than in Bangkok.

What began as my very first solo trip ended up becoming much more than that. It taught me that traveling alone isn't about packing every day with activities – it's about giving yourself the freedom to wander, slow down, and connect with a place on your own terms.

I know one thing for certain: I'll be coming back here again.

Thank you so much for reading! ❤️ I have a feeling this won't be my last solo travel story. I enjoyed this trip far more than I expected, and it's inspired me to turn these adventures into a series. Until next time, see you in the next destination!

Spanish photographer Laura Sales, who carries passion for portraits and analogue photography, recently experimented with dreamy, lo-fi style shots using the Diana F+ along with the LomoChrome Metropolis and Lomography Color Negative ISO 400. In this interview, she reveals how she connects spontaneously and intentionally with her models, and how she managed to maximize this camera’s potential.

Photos by Laura Sales with the Diana F+ and Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 400

Hi Laura, welcome to the Lomography Magazine! Could you briefly introduce yourself and tell us what you do?

I’m Laura, and I’m surrounded by film photography both at work and in my personal life. In my day-to-day work, I recommend film rolls and film cameras, so I’m lucky enough to constantly discover new materials and share this passion with others. Personally, what I enjoy photographing the most are portraits, because I love creating images that convey an emotion or tell a little story.

Photos by Laura Sales with the Diana F+ and Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 400

How did you get started in the world of analogue photography, and what appeals to you most about this medium?

I started when I was 17, when I enrolled in a degree program in analogue photography lab techniques. There, I learned how to develop film, make prints, and understand everything that happens from the moment you take a shot until you hold the final print in your hands. That’s where I fell in love with this medium.

Analogue photography always ends up surprising you, no matter how much you plan an image, there’s always something that’s beyond your control. I think that’s where much of its magic lies: learning to embrace the unexpected and understanding that often, the best photographs come precisely from what you hadn’t expected.

Photos by Laura Sales with the Diana F+ and Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 400

What inspires or excites you most about photographing people?

What interests me most is capturing something authentic. I’m not looking for someone to pose perfectly; rather, I want to find those small gestures or glances that appear when a person feels comfortable. I believe a good portrait says as much about the photographer as it does about the person in front of the camera, and that connection is what makes every session unique.

“Rather than being distracting, that lo-fi quality makes the photography feel much more emotional, and reinforces the idea that not everything has to be perfect to convey something.”

Tell us about your shooting sessions with the Diana F+. What was it like to work with this camera?

It was a fun experience because the Diana F+ forces you to let go of control. With other cameras, I usually visualize the result quite a bit before shooting, but with this one, I had to trust the process much more. That made the whole session more spontaneous, and encouraged me to experiment without overthinking things.

Which features of the Diana F+ stood out to you the most when taking photos?

It has a very unique way of interpreting light, with a soft focus, vignetting, and that signature imperfect look. It’s a camera that doesn’t strive for technical perfection, but rather to convey feelings.

Photos by Laura Sales with the Diana F+ and Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 400, LomoChrome Metropolis 120 ISO 100–400

Your portraits have a very spontaneous feel to them. Do you usually start a session with a specific idea in mind, or do you prefer to let your intuition and the moment guide you?

I usually have an initial idea or a few references, but I try not to cling to them too much. I like for the sessions to evolve naturally and to leave room for unexpected things to happen. Often, the photos I like best come from precisely those improvised moments.

Photo by Laura Sales with the Diana F+ and Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 400

The Diana’s dreamy, lo-fi aesthetic creates very distinctive results. How do you think this camera influenced the final look of your portraits?

I think the Diana F+ brought a very special atmosphere. Its imperfections give the images an almost dreamlike or nostalgic quality, and that fit very well with the way I wanted to approach the shoot. Rather than being distracting, that lo-fi quality makes the photography feel much more emotional, and reinforces the idea that not everything has to be perfect to convey something.

Is there a particular photo from this shoot that’s your favorite? Why?

Yes, definitely the accidental double exposure with the Barcelona skyline. The silhouette blends with the city in an almost dreamlike way, as if both scenes belonged to the same place. Some of the best results come when you simply let the camera work its magic.

Photo by Laura Sales with the Diana F+ and Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 400

Finally, do you have any future projects or creative ideas you’d like to share with our Community?

I want to keep developing personal projects focused on portraiture, and continue experimenting with different films and cameras. Ultimately, analogue photography has taught me that not everything has to turn out exactly as you imagined. It’s worth stepping out of your comfort zone and letting the process itself surprise you. I think that’s one of the most beautiful things about shooting on film.

Many thanks to Laura Sales for sharing her passion for portrait photography with us through these analogue shots taken with the Diana F+. If you'd like to follow Laura's work, be sure to check out her Instagram page.

We invited Wee Weeraya Zhang, former member of Thai girl group BNK48, to join us for this edition of A Day With. Armed with the Lomo'Instant Automat Glass, Wee shares a collection of instant photographs while opening up about her life these days, the memories she cherishes through film photography, and the ordinary moments that have come to mean the most to her. Let's take a look at her photos and hear the stories behind them.

© weewrya | Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Hello! I'm Wee. I'm 24 years old, and I'm currently working as an influencer and an independent actress.

© weewrya | Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Lately, I've been really into working out, especially rock climbing. I've also been trying to explore new activities whenever I can because I feel that stepping outside my comfort zone and trying new things helps me learn more about myself.

© weewrya | Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> Since I left the group, my life has changed quite a bit. I used to work closely with so many people and was always surrounded by friends. Now that we've each gone our own way, there are moments when I feel a little lonely, and I still miss everyone. But little by little, I've been learning to adjust and embrace this new chapter of my life.

© weewrya | Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> When it comes to film photography, I'm usually the one in front of the camera rather than behind it. But whenever I travel or experience a moment I truly want to remember, I always bring a film camera with me. For me, choosing to press the shutter on film means that moment is special enough to deserve a place on a roll of film. Then, when I see the photos after they're developed, it's like being transported back to that exact moment and reliving all the emotions I felt.

© weewrya | Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> For me, “a good photograph” is one that feels natural and unforced. I’m drawn to images that are honest, approachable, and not overly polished. That’s also why I love the charm of film photography – it has a sincerity and authenticity that feels truly genuine.

© weewrya | Lomo'Instant Automat Glass

> One of my favorite moments of the day is actually riding on the back of a motorcycle (it sounds a little funny, doesn't it?). Bangkok traffic can be pretty bad, so I often listen to music while we're on the road. It may seem like an ordinary part of the day, but it's when I feel most connected to myself. It's quiet, peaceful, and I really cherish those moments.

A big thank you to Wee for inviting us into her everyday life and sharing these beautiful instant moments with us. You can keep up with her on Instagram: weewrya, Facebook: vmoho and TikTok: weewrya.

Some lenses just have a personality, and the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens is one of them. As Photographer Yiran notes: it helps you step out of the current, and brings you back to a creative flow. She took it out to the woods, the park, a small village – no fancy setups, just natural light. Here's what happened when she let this lens do its thing.

© Yiran | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Hi, Yiran! Welcome to the Lomography Magazine. Could you start by telling us a little about yourself and what you usually shoot?

Thank you for having me! I'm truly happy to be here and to share my work. Most of my time is spent photographing. I love wandering through streets, parks, and cities, capturing natural, relaxed moments. I also share real-life shooting experiences and my thoughts on light and narrative online.

Is this your first time using a Lomography product? Have you worked with manual or art lenses before?

Yes, this is my first time. I've never used a manual or art lens prior to this.

© Yiran | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

What was your first impression of the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens when you held it? And how did that impression evolve after shooting with it?

This lens has serious character. I was drawn to its look right away, but once I started shooting, the optical quality and the way it renders images completely won me over, even more than the design.

© Yiran | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

The Joseph Petzval has a very distinct personality: the swirly bokeh, the atmospheric feel, the retro color rendering, the manual focus. It slows you down. It makes you observe, judge, and compose with intention.

For me, this lens isn't just about beautiful images, it's a deliberately chosen limitation. And that limitation pushes you to express more. It's not a “productivity tool”. It's an expressive tool.

Can you walk us through the time you spent with this lens? Where did you take it, and what did you shoot?

I brought the Joseph Petzval into an autumn metasequoia forest, a park, and a small village – I mainly shot portraits. Shooting in backlit conditions among the trees, I also captured some video. The swirl bokeh turned the out-of-focus leaves into soft, dreamy spirals, adding an unmistakable atmosphere. I worked entirely with natural light, quietly observing how the lens handled color and bokeh in daylight, and documented those quiet, relaxed autumn moments.

© Yiran | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Was there any particular scene or frame that truly amazed you during the shoot?

Honestly, almost every frame surprised me. But what amazed me most? The video footage. Seeing the Petzval's signature swirl in motion was something else.

What are your favorite features of this lens in actual use?

The swirl bokeh and the vintage, atmospheric color palette.

© Yiran | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

How does this lens differ from others you've used in terms of visual storytelling?

Other lenses give me “correctness” and let me “record quickly”. The Petzval gives me a “perspective” and makes me “narrate actively”. This lens demands focus, judgment, and choice. It pulls you into a creative flow state.

When would you reach for this lens again? What kind of projects or assignments do you think it's best suited for?

If I ever start a long-term personal project, something like “city streets” or “a single village,” I would absolutely use this lens again. Especially for series that need a consistent visual style. I want to use a steady, unified visual language to document ordinary, everyday scenes over time. The kind of frames that are easy to overlook, but quietly real.

© Yiran | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Finally, what would you say to other creators who are curious about this lens?

We live in a time flooded with images – polished, virtual, filtered. The essence of photography is slowly diluted by algorithms and trends. The Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 is more than a lens. It helps you step out of that current. It brings you back to a creative flow; more quiet thinking, less restless anxiety. When you shoot with it, you follow your own rhythm. You don't get trapped in someone else's idea of what looks good. I hope you can also enjoy this state of creation – true to yourself.

© Yiran | Shot with the Joseph Petzval 55 f/1.7 Focus-coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Thank you to Yiran for sharing her honest thoughts and beautiful work. To see more of her visual storytelling, follow her on Bilibili and step into her world of light and shadow.

In this feature, we catch up with portrait photographer Green, also known as midori.pix), who recently put the Lomo MC-A to the test across two portrait sessions in completely different settings. Join us as he shares his experience with the camera, his thoughts after shooting with it, and, of course, the photographs that came out of the experience.

© midori.pix

Hi, Green! Could you briefly introduce yourself and tell us how you got into photography?

Hello everyone! I'm Green, a.k.a midori.pix, a portrait and graduation photographer. My style leans toward warm, soft, nostalgic images with the timeless feel of classic film photography. My journey into photography began when my older brother gave me a camera and a few lenses to experiment with. From there, I started exploring different genres of photography, and before I knew it, more than ten years had passed.

About five years ago, I discovered the unique charm of vintage film colors and classic film stocks. I was drawn to their distinctive look and the creative challenge they offered. Since then, I've been shooting film consistently because I want every graduation portrait and profile photo I take to feel a little different, carrying the nostalgic atmosphere and timeless character of traditional film photography.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 | Model: dinipts

What was your first impression of the Lomo MC-A? And after spending some time shooting with it, how would you describe its character?

My first impression was that it's incredibly compact, charming, and has a classic look. It immediately gave me the feel of a point-and-shoot camera, small enough to slip into a shirt pocket and easy to carry anywhere. But once I actually started shooting with it, I realized it has a character I'd describe as “raw, yet beautifully balanced.” The colors are rich and vibrant, with subtle vignetting around the edges that gives images that unmistakable Lomography look.

What really surprised me, though, was how beautifully it renders portraits in natural light. Skin tones come out soft and smooth without looking harsh at all. For such a compact camera, it also packs in some fun creative features, like double exposure, which makes it perfect for anyone who enjoys experimenting with more expressive, artistic photographs.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 | Model: dinipts

Where did you take the Lomo MC-A, and what did you choose to photograph?

I actually took the MC-A out for two separate portrait sessions in two completely different locations, each with its own atmosphere and a different model, so the results had a very distinct feel.

The first shoot was in Talad Noi. I took my model on a relaxed street portrait walk through the neighborhood's narrow alleyways and old buildings. It was all about strolling around, camera in hand, waiting for the right moments and shooting naturally. I focused on capturing the afternoon sunlight as it spilled across weathered concrete walls and vintage cars. The camera's character complemented the location perfectly, giving the images a raw, vintage aesthetic that really enhanced the mood of the surroundings.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 | Model: dinipts

The second session took place at the Chatuchak Fish Market. This time, I wanted to experiment with indoor lighting and a completely different atmosphere. I captured candid moments of another model quietly admiring the aquariums, with the neon lights and reflections from the glass tanks falling across her face. The Lomo MC-A rendered those layers of light beautifully, giving the images a soft, mysterious, and almost cinematic quality.

Across both shoots, my approach was the same: keep everything spontaneous and embrace a true point-and-shoot mindset. I didn't rely on any elaborate techniques or complicated setups, just the camera, the moment, and whatever unfolded naturally in front of me.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

The Lomo MC-A comes with Auto, Aperture Priority, and Manual shooting modes. Do you think having this level of control makes the camera easier to use?

Absolutely. It makes shooting both easier and a lot more enjoyable. When you're out walking with a camera, the light is constantly changing. On days when I just want to raise the camera and capture the moment, I simply switch to Auto or Aperture Priority mode. I can open up the aperture for a beautifully soft background, let the camera handle the rest, and confidently catch those spontaneous, unplanned moments.

“The camera's character complemented the location perfectly, giving the images a raw, vintage aesthetic that really enhanced the mood of the surroundings.”

But when I step into a darker alley or want to create a dramatic backlit silhouette, I can easily switch to Manual mode and dial everything in myself. That flexibility means the MC-A can adapt to almost any shooting style or creative idea, which is something I really appreciate.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

The Lomo MC-A features Autofocus, Manual Zone Focus, manual ISO settings, and easy-to-use Exposure Compensation. Do you prefer controlling everything yourself, or do you usually let the camera take over?

I'd say it's more like the camera and I share the creative process, though we occasionally have our disagreements. One thing I almost always like to control myself is Exposure Compensation, because I prefer my images to be slightly underexposed. It gives them the moody, melancholic atmosphere that's become part of my style.

As for the autofocus, it's genuinely smart and performs just as you'd expect from a modern point-and-shoot. That said, it does have its stubborn moments. In very low light or when the background is particularly busy, the camera sometimes seems to hesitate, almost as if it's asking itself, “Wait...what should I focus on?” The shutter locks, and no matter how many times I press it, it simply refuses to take the shot.

When that happens, I just switch over to Manual Zone Focus and take control myself. Honestly, I don't mind it at all – it adds a bit of personality to the experience. Those quirky moments keep you engaged and remind you that you're interacting with a camera, not just pressing a button.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

What was your reaction when you saw the results for the first time?

“That's the film look!” Point-and-shoot, simply as that! The images look very lively. The lens delivers beautiful colors, retains plenty of detail, and produces images with balanced contrast and smooth tonal transitions. There is a touch of the crispness you'd expect from a compact camera, but it still feels very natural.

With a maximum shutter speed of 1/500, you'll sometimes want to shoot with a wider aperture, but that's never really an issue. What impressed me most, though, was the camera's metering. Whether I was shooting into the light, using flash, or relying solely on available light, the exposure was consistently accurate. It handled backlit scenes especially well, giving me exactly the results I was hoping for.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

What kinds of situations or occasions is the Lomo MC-A best suited for?

I'd say it's at its best from around 4 p.m. through sunset. The light during those hours is simply beautiful, and it's hard to take a bad photo. It's also the perfect camera to keep with you as an everyday companion, whether you're wandering around on a day off, café hopping, or spending time with friends during a graduation pre-shoot.

It's also a lot of fun to experiment with Double Exposure. You can pass the camera around, take turns composing and shooting, and create something together without worrying about getting everything technically perfect. The result is a collection of photographs that feel stylish, full of character, and unlike anyone else's.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

If you were to take the Lomo MC-A out for another photo walk, what song would you choose as the soundtrack for the day?

I'd go with Plastic Love by Mariya Takeuchi. It's a classic Japanese city pop track from the '80s with a funky groove, but there's a subtle sense of melancholy beneath it. That combination perfectly complements the Lomo MC-A's vibrant colors and vintage character. Put on that song, wander around with the camera, and keep pressing the shutter. You'll be so immersed in the experience that you'll lose track of time.

Do you have any advice for people who are interested in trying the Lomo MC-A for themselves?

I’d say, “Relax and just enjoy the process.” This camera wasn’t made to produce perfectly sharp images like the latest smartphones. Some photos might come out blurry, or you might accidentally create a double exposure that leaves you wondering what happened, but that’s exactly where the charm and creativity of point-and-shoot film photography come from.

Allow yourself to experiment, make mistakes, and discover what the camera can do. Once you embrace that process, you’ll start to appreciate and fall in love with this unique kind of photographic experience.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

For anyone who’s preparing for a graduation shoot or looking for a photographer to capture stylish film-inspired portraits with a warm and natural mood, feel free to check out my work, have a chat, ask for advice, or inquire about availability through my Instagram: midori.pix.

A huge thank you to Green for sharing his experience with the Lomo MC-A with us. The photographs he created are truly stunning and showcase the camera’s unique character so beautifully. Stay tuned to see who we’ll be interviewing next!
