Ishmael Claxton is an African-American photographer now based in Dublin, Ireland who has been utilizing the various tones and hues from LomoChrome films to express different ideas on race, identity and meaning. One of his series, Garden of Eden, uses LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400 film to document youth and moments of transition.

Meanwhile, in a recent project, Dead Zoo in Blue, he photographed the Dead Zoo Lab at The National Museum of Ireland and shot the entire project on LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100–400 35 mm film. The work raises questions about decolonization within museum spaces, with a special focus on the dismantling of the Dead Zoo. We talked to Ishmael about his work, the messages he wants to create through his practice and and why he chooses to shoot with LomoChrome films.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Hi Ishmael, please tell us a bit about yourself?

I am a visual artist and photographer based in Dublin. I grew up in New York City in the 1990s and early 2000s, in a neighborhood that was first hit by drugs and later by waves of gentrification. Watching a place change that quickly shaped how I think about images, memory, and who gets to remain visible as cities transform.

My work moves between photography, installation, and curating with others. I photograph people, spaces, and objects that already carry histories. A museum display, a street corner, or a quiet portrait can all reveal traces of power, migration, and belonging. Photography became the way I sort through those layers. I often mix staged images with documentary moments because real life rarely sits neatly in one category.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Over the past few years my work has been recognized through several awards and exhibitions. In 2023, I was shortlisted for the LensCulture Editors’ Pick. In 2024, my work was shortlisted for both the Taylor Wessing Photographic Portrait Prize and the Royal Photographic Society International Photography Exhibition 166. In 2025, I was selected as one of the 100 Fine Art Photographers of Tomorrow for the Shutter Hub OPEN exhibition at the University of Cambridge.

My work has been shown at places including the Museum of Literature Ireland, PhotoMuseum Ireland, the National Concert Hall, the RHA Annual Exhibition, the Hunt Museum, the Royal Ulster Academy, the Irish Georgian Society, Russborough House, and Gallery X. I have also taken part in residencies that helped shape my practice, including PhotoMuseum Ireland, the Center for Visual Storytelling in Santa Fe, Cow House Studios, 3 Walls Gallery, Culture Vulture Autumn AIR, and Queens Collective. I am also a co-founder of ÍOVA Collective, a photographer-led group in Ireland that supports image makers and creates space for new work.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton

How did you get into shooting film?

I first touched film in an after school program when I was in junior high school. We had a small darkroom and I remember watching an image slowly appear in the developer tray. That moment stayed with me. Years later, I came back to film after two events happened close together. A digital hard drive crashed and I lost years of images. Not long after that, my family home burned down. The only photographs that survived both events were negatives and prints.

“Color is one of my favorite tools in photography. Changing the film stock can completely shift how we see the world.”

That experience changed the way I thought about photography. Film lasts. It sits quietly in a box and waits for you. When I returned to New York, I started taking classes at the Bushwick Community Darkroom, where I was mentored by Lucia Rollow. That time in the darkroom gave me a deeper respect for the craft and the patience film demands. Since then, I have trusted it in a different way.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Tell us about this project and how it came about?

I often work with Lomography film stocks because their color shifts push the image somewhere unexpected. The film itself becomes part of the language of the work. For a series called Garden of Eden in Purple, I used purple-toned film to photograph youth culture and moments of transition. I also used LomoChrome Metropolis to photograph crumbling housing and empty buildings during the housing crisis.

Color can carry meaning before a viewer even reads the photograph. For queer portraits, I leaned into purple again because it holds softness and tension at the same time. With turquoise and blue tones I began developing projects like Dead Zoo in Blue and Mood Indigo. These works move through museums, archives, and portraiture to question how race, identity, and bodies have been classified or displayed inside institutions.

Garden of Eden Series by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

What made you want to shoot the Dead Zoo in Blue project using only LomoChrome Turquoise film?

Color is one of my favorite tools in photography. Changing the film stock can completely shift how we see the world. Turquoise film bends color just enough to make familiar scenes feel slightly strange. Skin tones, skies, and shadows all move away from what we expect. That shift is useful to me. It interrupts our habits of looking. When an entire body of work is made with the same palette, it builds its own atmosphere and the viewer steps into that world.

Most of the Lomography film I use comes from John Gunn Camera Shop. The Gunn’s family have become an important part of the photography community in Dublin. A few years ago, I actually asked if they would consider stocking Lomography film. They brought it in, and since then more photographers here have started experimenting with it. It has been nice to see that small shift help grow a local film community.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

If the LomoChrome Turquoise film you used for your project, Dead Zoo in Blue, had a soundtrack, what song would capture its mood best?

When I look at those colors, I hear jazz. The first song that comes to mind is Mood Indigo by Duke Ellington. I also think of the quiet intensity of Nina Simone and the spiritual depth of Alice Coltrane. Those sounds carry blue in the same way the film does. Slow, reflective, and full of feeling.

Garden of Eden Series by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

What’s coming up for you in 2026?

2026 has already been an incredibly rewarding year and many of the projects I began developing over the last few years have finally taken shape. One of the biggest has been Mood Indigo, an ongoing portrait series inspired by the Irish phrase “duine gorm”, a historical term once used to describe Black people that literally translates as blue person”. Originally conceived as a series of 100 portraits, I decided to expand the project to 120 portraits, marking each year of Irish independence and allowing the work to continue growing beyond a fixed endpoint. Using specialized blue tinted film, the project explores identity, belonging, and contemporary Black life in Ireland.

As of August 2026, I have photographed 118 people of color from across Ireland, ranging in age from 6 to 85 years old. The project has introduced me to extraordinary individuals from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences, and those conversations have become just as important as the photographs themselves. I am excited to see where the final portraits, and the relationships formed through the project, will lead in the years ahead.

Earlier this year, I also released Dead Zoo in Blue, a project that began during my African Artist Residency at Photo Museum Ireland in collaboration with the National Museum of Ireland – Natural History. The work examines museum collections through the lens of colonial history, asking how bodies, objects, and narratives have been classified, preserved, and interpreted over time. The accompanying publication was launched at The Library Project in Dublin.

Garden of Eden Series by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Another highlight of the year was curating Black Noise at Gallery X. The exhibition brought together 22 Black artists from across Ireland and became far more than an exhibition. We expanded the programme to include a roundtable discussion exploring how the arts can build stronger communities, a live music jam session, poetry readings, contemporary dance performances, a collaborative zine-making workshop, and concluded with a healing circle. Seeing artists, audiences, and community groups come together across different disciplines made it one of the most meaningful projects I have worked on.

Looking ahead to the remainder of 2026, I will be co-curating the 7th annual ÍOVA Photography Collective Culture Night exhibition at REDS Gallery this September, continuing our commitment to showcasing emerging and established photographic practices from across Ireland.

I am also developing a new collaborative exhibition, Alternative Methods, which will open at Tøn Gallery in November. Created alongside four female artists, the project explores alternative approaches to curatorial practice by integrating pedagogy into the exhibition-making process. Rather than presenting a finished exhibition assembled by a single curator, we are collectively undertaking studio visits, conversations, and shared decision making, allowing the exhibition itself to emerge through collaboration and dialogue.

Dead Zoo in Blue, Ishmael Claxton is available now from The Library Project. To see more of Ishmael's work, visit his website.

Shortly after the launch of the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera, Lomography Thailand sent the camera, preloaded with Lady Grey ISO 400 film, to Guy (dopamine.51) to put it to the test. Let’s take a look at how Guy created half-frame stories and captured the old town side of Bangkok in light and shadow.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

Hi, Guy! Could you please introduce yourself and tell us how you first got into photography?

Hi, everyone, my name is Guy. My interest in photography started with my mother, who has always loved taking photos. We had film cameras at home, along with lots of photo albums with photos of important moments in our lives. Around 2018, I came across an old film camera, so I decided to give it a try. I was drawn to the soft, warm tones and unique look of film photography. Around the same time, film photography was making a comeback here in Thailand, which inspired me to start learning more seriously about photography.

Currently, I work as a portrait photographer, shooting a variety of projects including conceptual portraits, graduation photos, cosplay, and idol photography. I pay close attention to selecting props, matching the colors of outfits with the locations, and choosing the right type of film for each shoot. I work with color film and motion picture film, as well as techniques such as flash and colored lighting, to create an atmosphere that suits each project.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

Where did you take this camera for a spin? Was there any theme or concept behind the shoot?

I chose to shoot around the Phra Nakhon side of Bangkok, particularly in Charoen Krung, Yaowarat, and Song Wat, as these all are familiar places for me. I wanted to shoot in the evening, especially when the shops were starting to open and the streets were filled with vendors, tourists, and changing natural light. This created beautiful contrasts between light and shadow.

For the concept, I wanted the two frames to have a connection, whether by telling the same story or creating a contrast between the two images.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

What was your first impression of this camera? Have you used a half-frame film camera before?

First of all, I was really happy to see that it’s a half-frame version of the Simple Use Camera and that it can be reloaded with new films, which is something I really like. The camera is very compact and lightweight, comes with a wide-angle lens and a built-in flash, making it very easy to carry around. I also really like the orange-and-black body.

I’ve used an Olympus Pen EE before. It’s a really fun half-frame camera to shoot with, although one downside is that it doesn’t have a built-in flash, so photos can turn out a little dark in low-light situations. After trying the Half-frame Simple Use, I found it much easier and more convenient to use. The built-in flash means I don’t have to worry as much when shooting in low light. It gives me peace of mind knowing that I can take it anywhere and still get good results.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

What was your impression when you got the results back from the lab?

The lens is sharper than I expected, with great detail and clarity. The film has nice grain and contrasts. Overall, the results turned out just as I had envisioned. I was really impressed with how well it performed.

“I wanted to shoot in the evening, especially when the shops were starting to open and the streets were filled with vendors, tourists, and changing natural light. This created beautiful contrasts between light and shadow.”

When shooting in half-frame format, did you find yourself seeing things differently? How did your approach to photography change compared to shooting in full frame?

For me, it feels quite similar because I usually shoot in portrait orientation anyway. The main difference is thinking about how to pair the two frames and how they can connect to tell a story. It makes shooting more fun and gives me more room to incorporate creative ideas.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

What do you like most about this camera, and how do you think it differs from digital or other film cameras you’ve used?

I love the fact that it's very easy to use. It's a half-frame camera that lets you take a lot of photos, and you can even reload it with different films, which makes it great value for money. The wide-angle lens allows you to shoot in narrow spaces. The built-in flash is another feature I really like, as it adds more fun and dimension to the images. Compared to larger professional cameras, I also find that people in front of the camera tend to feel more relaxed and less self-conscious when I’m shooting with it.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

If you had the chance to use this camera again, where would you take it, or what kind of moments would you want to capture first?

I’d like to use it in a wedding, where everyone is dressed up and looking their best. With its user-friendly design, I think it would be great for capturing warm moments with family and the bride and groom, as well as the fun atmosphere among the guests. I believe that if I handed the camera around and let everyone take photos, we’d end up with a collection full of memorable moments.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

Were there any particular photos you were especially impressed with from this camera? Could you tell us the story behind them?

The first photo is of a tuk-tuk in the middle of an intersection. I stood there waiting for quite a while because I wanted to capture the moment when there was only one vehicle in the middle of the intersection. Then, unexpectedly, the tuk-tuk driver ran a red light, and I ended up getting this shot! Hahaha.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

The second photo is of a young male model who happens to be my regular barber. We often talked about photography whenever I went to get a haircut, so this time I finally asked him to be my model. Hahaha. He was really happy about it – after hearing me talk about photography so much, he said it was time for him to give it a try himself.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

If you had the chance to take the Half-frame Simple Use out for another shoot, what song would you choose as the soundtrack?

I’d choose Perfect Timing by Ray Saetta. The beat and vocals fit perfectly with the atmosphere of walking around and taking photos, especially when shooting in black and white.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

Do you have any advice or tips for anyone trying the Half-frame Simple Use for the first time?

I’d say it’s really easy to use. It has a built-in flash, is convenient to take with you when traveling, and offers great value for money. Plus, you can reload it with new rolls of film. I also think it makes a great gift for a friend or partner, or a fun camera to have at events where everyone can take turns using it.

Lastly, I’d love for everyone to follow my work on Instagram at dopamine.51. If you’d like to chat, ask for advice, or are interested in hiring me for film or digital photography, as well as camera and photography gear reviews, feel free to get in touch. I hope everyone enjoys taking photos. Thank you!

Big thanks to Guy for sharing his work captured with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera!

As it turns out, poetry and photography share a deeply common language. Netherlands-based creator Nikki, also known as Satellite June, proves exactly that in her new book, The Many Deaths of My Mother. Armed with a typewriter and a collection of film cameras, she set out to confront her grief. Whether in black and white or color, medium or 35 mm format, the reader gets to see images turned deeply personal. In this article, she opens up about the cathartic effects of making art.

© @ satellitejune

Hi, Nikki! It is so lovely to meet you. I'm really happy to have the chance to interview you on your recent book, The Many Deaths of My Mother. But first, could you briefly introduce yourself to the readers of Lomography Magazine?

Hi! I'm Nikki, a film photographer based in the Netherlands, working under the artist name Satellite June. I love finding magic in everyday life – the quiet, often overlooked moments that ask you to slow down and look again. In my work, I build bridges between art and mental health, using photography as a way to explore vulnerability and inner landscapes that are not always easy to put into words.

© @ satellitejune

Your book is a beautiful homage to both poetry and photography. Tell us, when did the idea of combining these two media start to take shape?

It all happened very naturally, actually; a regular day for me is starting the day writing my morning pages and going for a walk. During that walk, I always look around me to find magic in everyday life; shadows that are dancing, beautiful shapes, colors that spark my interest. I always have a little camera in my bag everywhere I go, so I can capture a moment that makes me feel something. My book is a combination of both these habits of mine.

© @ satellitejune

Looking back, I realized I photographed during the periods when I couldn't explain my feelings. The images helped me understand what I was going through. When life became a little lighter again, the words followed naturally. Writing poetry became another way of processing those experiences. Bringing photography and poetry together in the book felt inevitable – they complete one another.

Throughout the book, you use solely analogue photos. Why did you decide to use film instead of, say, digital images?

From the moment I started taking photographs, I've done everything with an analogue camera. I never even tried doing it digitally; I fell in love with film straight away. I loved the feeling of being in the moment and learned to trust myself and my vision a lot this way. I am a big fan of the grainy, nostalgic feel film gives my images; it matches the dreamy vibe I like to create.

© @ satellitejune

When browsing through your published work, we find many self-portraits. Why was it important for you to have them accompany your poems?

Photography became an instinctive way of processing what I couldn't put into words. The self-portraits were never about showing myself to other people; they were about finding myself again. During periods where I felt like I was simply surviving, the camera helped me to ask, “How am I, really?” Those photographs became a quiet visual diary of my inner world.

© @ satellitejune

In the introduction to your book, you wrote that after finishing it, you “feel that you have learned how to hold living loss differently”. Can you tell us more about how completing this creative piece helped you navigate and process grief?

The idea for the book came to life when I was browsing through my ten years' worth of photographs and noticed a common thread: I photographed to deal with overwhelming feelings, and in a lot of them, that was grief. When I couldn’t find the words, I turned to photography. Looking back now, I can see that grief has been a major part of my life, and I think most people experience forms of grief throughout their lives as well.

“Bringing photography and poetry together in the book felt inevitable – they complete one another.”

Sometimes it’s a big wave of grief, sometimes it’s a little splash. Grieving is way more common than we think; it’s just something that isn’t talked about a lot when it’s not the “obvious” kind of grief when somebody dies. There is also grief in ending a relationship, missing an old version of yourself, missing a time in your life, missing friendships that changed as you got older, etc.

So, I guess, from making the book, I learned that taking photographs is a way for me to deal with heavy feelings. In my photography, I capture both the hard times, as well as the beautiful, mundane things, and it works really soothing for my mind.

© @ satellitejune

Loss and grief are deeply personal. What made you share these vulnerable feelings with the world?

It took me a long time to find the courage to share this work. The photographs were made during a period when I was trying to survive rather than create. They were never intended as a project; they were a way of holding on to myself.

Over time, I realized that the title, The Many Deaths of My Mother , could belong to anyone. You could replace the word mother with health, love, home, or the future you imagined. The details of our stories may differ, but the feelings they carry are often remarkably similar.

Sharing this work is my way of creating space for those feelings. I hope the book offers recognition, comfort, and permission to grieve experiences that are rarely acknowledged. If my vulnerability allows someone else to recognize their own experience, to find language for feelings they haven't been able to name, or simply to feel a little less alone, then sharing it feels worthwhile. I believe that the more we allow ourselves to speak honestly about grief, the less isolated it becomes.

© @ satellitejune

Since we have a lot of photography geeks reading our magazine, we have to ask: what cameras did you choose to work with for this project? Was there any Lomography gear involved?

Most of my work is shot on my main camera – the Canon AE-1. In addition to that, I used a Mamiya C3, a Nikon F3, a Polaroid Spirit 600 CL, Kodak Ektar H35, and the Lomo’Instant Square Glass Camera. The photographs in the book are a compilation of my work from the past 10 years, so I used a lot of different cameras along the way.

© @ satellitejune | Shot on Lomo’Instant Square Glass Camera

How about the film stocks? We're pretty sure we spot some Lomography Redscale in there!

Hah, that’s right! I love the Redscale film stock. I love how it feels really warm, but also otherworldly, like you’re entering a dream world. Besides that, I used a lot of different films: Kodak Gold 200, Cinestill 800T, Kodak Portra 160/400/800, Fujifilm 400, Ilford HP5, and Polaroid.

I love to keep on experimenting and finding the films that fit the mood I want to photograph. Switching between cooler/warmer tones, or more greenish or yellowish tones, adds more depth to my work. I like to think that I “edit” my photographs before I even press the shutter. Choosing the camera and film stock is already part of the creative process; they determine the atmosphere long before the image exists.

© @ satellitejune | Shot on Lomography Redscale 35mm

Poetry is obviously a massive part of the book as well. Can you tell us a bit about your writing process? Is it purely spontaneous, or perhaps more structured and organized?

A while ago, I got a typewriter as a gift from a friend, and I love the feeling of writing on it. The sound is lovely as well, and it fits my analogue approach in my work. It helps you to be in the moment more, to just focus on writing. During the book-making process, something magical happened: on some days, I could just feel that there was a poem that needed to be written. I would sit down and start writing, and it would just flow easily. I couldn’t stop thinking about the book Big Magic by Elizabeth Gilbert when that happened.

© @ satellitejune

Last, but not least – can we expect any similar projects from you in the future?

I'm interested in expanding beyond photography and exploring how grief, care, and connection can be experienced through different materials and rituals. I'm not entirely sure where that research will lead me yet, but that's exactly what excites me.

Stay updated on Satellite June’s projects by following her Instagram Page and definitely check out her new book here!

We have invited @filmlife_ww to use the Lomo MC-A Film Camera as a creative tool. Paired with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800, he expands his lens from everyday street photography to the preservation of local Hong Kong culture.

By documenting vanishing collective memories like neon signs, he explores the delicate balance between “imagery and boundaries” in street photography. Through his visuals, he attempts to freeze the city's lingering warmth, inviting readers to notice and record the seemingly ordinary scenes that carry profound cultural weight.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Hello @filmlife_ww! Welcome back to Lomography Magazine! What have you been up to lately?

Hello everyone, it’s great to connect with you all again! I’d like to thank Lomography for lending me the Lomo MC-A film camera, and share this body of work with your readers. Lately, I’ve been trying hard to strike a balance between work and life. Over the past six months, I’ve stepped back from spontaneous, cinematic street shoots to focus more on documentary-style projects. I’ve also been attending more photography exhibitions and community events to seek fresh inspiration.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Please share some moments from your time with the camera. Where did you go, and what did you capture?

For this project, I decided to shift my photographic perspective from local neighborhoods to cultural preservation. The series also includes plenty of snapshots capturing the diverse facets of daily city life and community rhythms. Neon signs, dai pai dongs (open-air food stalls), mahjong parlors, nightclubs, bamboo scaffolding, and old-school market stalls all found a place before my lens.

These elements are scenes that Hong Kongers take for granted – things we pass by on the street that quietly blend into every corner of the city. Because they are so familiar, people might not pay close attention to them. However, these seemingly ordinary sights, objects, bricks, and tiles carry Hong Kong’s cultural heritage and historical context.

The stories behind the neon signs are particularly worth mentioning. The lingering shadows of the nightclubs on Portland Street in Mong Kok bear witness to Hong Kong's bustling, glamorous nightlife of the 1980s and 90s, recording how crowds used to converge under the neon glow. Moving over to Central, “Ser Wong Fun” has preserved its century-old traditional craft since its founding in 1895. Starting out with a single bowl of snake soup, it has not only kept classic Cantonese flavors alive but has also become an unforgettable landmark in Soho.

Meanwhile, the historic “Tak Hing Dried Seafood” in Yau Ma Tei protects the warmth of Hong Kongers in a different way, building trust through meticulously prepared soups and an enduring reputation, quietly serving the neighborhood for over half a century with low-key yet steadfast dedication. Each story, shaped by time, silently pieces together the silhouette of this city.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

What was your first impression of the Lomo MC-A?

The moment I held it, I was immediately drawn to its appearance. The metal casing felt high-quality, and when paired with the black leather, the body looked textured yet stylish – a highly recognizable design. The most striking detail is undoubtedly the Lomography manifesto engraved on the camera body: All those who stand before a lens are equal. This adds a distinct personality to the Lomo MC-A.

Lomography has always been a symbol of rebellion and individualism in the film world, and this camera puts that entirely on display.

“As the dismantling continues, perhaps one day we will have to walk into a museum just to see the glow of neon.”

How did it perform during casual, everyday shooting?

To be honest, as someone accustomed to traditional manual SLRs, it took me a moment to adapt to the Lomo MC-A because it is incredibly lightweight. However, both beginners and experienced users can pick it up with ease. While being compact and portable, the MC-A features an LCD screen that displays the frame count and focus mode, allowing me to keep track of shooting info at a glance.

Before the shoot, I was really looking forward to seeing its image quality and how it differed from traditional film cameras. For this series, I used two high-contrast films: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400. The night performance was particularly surprising.

Both the color tones and depth of field delivered a texture very close to that of a traditional film camera. As a 32 mm fixed focal length camera, its wide-angle performance is also excellent. The only minor drawback is that the camera occasionally turns off automatically during shooting; it would be even better if this point could be slightly improved.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Do you have any advice for fellow photography enthusiasts who want to get closer to their subjects in street photography?

I have thought about this question repeatedly. Finding a balance between taking a good photo and respecting boundaries is a challenge every street photographer must face. In my experience, when shooting indoor scenes, like the dynamics of people inside a cha chaan teng (Hong Kong-style café), I usually patronize the shop first and take photos on the premise so as not to disrupt their business.

One of the keys to street photography is speed. A great piece of work is often born in the blink of an eye. Therefore, before pressing the shutter, observe first, compose the shot in your mind, and then shoot decisively when the timing is right, thereby minimizing interference with the subject. For beginners, you can start with a longer focal length lens to shoot from a comfortable “social distance”. As you gain experience, you can gradually switch to a wide-angle prime lens, learning to observe the subtle interactions between people and their environment, blending into the scene, and judging the right moment to capture it.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

The Lomo MC-A offers features like autofocus, manual zone focusing, manual ISO, and exposure compensation. Did you control these settings yourself during the shoot, or did you let the camera decide?

The camera's wide array of adjustable features is undoubtedly one of its greatest strengths. When doing street photography, having higher manual control offers greater flexibility, so I preferred using manual settings for most of the shoot. Because street photography is easily affected by changing environments and lighting, manually adjusting the aperture, ISO, and focus allows me to flexibly set the most appropriate parameters based on the subject.

That said, I also tried the autofocus function during the shoot; for instance, in the shot taken at Pak Bo Tong in Sham Shui Po, the subject came out very sharp, and the result was quite good. Additionally, the camera is equipped with a multiple exposure function. This versatile design gave me even more creative options when it came to composition.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Which photograph from this series is your favorite, and why?

That’s a tough one! There are quite a few pieces from this series that I really love. But if I had to choose the one that left the deepest impression, it would have to be this one. The photo was taken at dusk, capturing the flow of the crowd heading home after work just as the city’s daily hustle was winding down. In the frame, the long, stretching staircase and handrail pull the viewer's eye toward an unseen horizon, making the entire movement feel like an extension of a singular rhythm.

Converging to the exact same beat within that narrow, confined space, the crowd weaves together Hong Kong's fast-paced yet orderly stride, beautifully showcasing the inherent tension and energy of the city's pulse.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

If you had to choose a song to represent the feeling of shooting with the Lomo MC-A, what would it be?

I would choose Eason Chan's Salon. The Lomo MC-A gives me a highly creative shooting experience, it feels grounded yet rebellious, projecting an unconstrained attitude. It embodies the spirit of living in the moment and embracing reality, reminding us to experience life with heightened sensitivity and to use our cameras to record unpolished fragments of existence.

Just as “Salon” uses photography as a metaphor for life, the key lies in capturing the sheer density of living. When we learn to cherish the present and freeze each moment in time, life becomes real, rather than vanishing into thin air like smoke.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Lastly, is there anything else you’d like to share with us? Any upcoming projects or parting words for our readers?

First, let me share a fun piece of trivia about neon signs. The rise of neon lights in Hong Kong began after World War II. With the rapid development of post-war industry, businesses of all kinds – restaurants, nightclubs, pawn shops – used neon signs as advertising tools, reaching a golden era in the 1980s and 90s. Some local neon signs even set Guinness World Records. In 1973, the National neon sign on the exterior wall of the Majestic Theatre in Jordan was made using over 4,000 neon tubes, becoming the largest in the world at the time. In 1982, the Citizen Watches neon sign in Causeway Bay broke the record with tubes stretching a total of three miles. By 1990, the Panasonic neon sign broke the record yet again, becoming the longest neon sign globally at the time before it was officially retired in 2021.

Today, the number of neon signs in Hong Kong has plummeted to around 224, with about 139 in Kowloon and 85 on Hong Kong Island. Over the past five years, more than 16,000 signs (including neon ones) have been removed, turning what was once a brilliant city icon into a vanishing cultural heritage. It feels as though some landscapes are destined to become specimens of a bygone era.

Online commentators often note that Hong Kong is no longer what it used to be, losing its uniqueness to homogenization. While conceptualizing this project, I couldn't help but wonder: under the crushing gears of time, what can truly remain unchanged for half a century? Some places have witnessed such beauty that people form deep attachments to them, making it difficult to let go even when they become unrecognizable. Since we cannot reverse the tides of time, we can use images as a form of preservation, reclaiming those familiar scenes through the lens. This body of work is precisely about holding onto the city's remaining warmth and defining a Hong Kong that belongs to me.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

“Act as a phonograph – that is the finest creed for any creative youth.” I would also like to invite our readers to become active participants in cultural preservation. Pay a little more attention during your daily commutes, and document the city's unique symbols in your own way. What truly deserves to be protected is often not just the imminent demolition making the news, but those seemingly ordinary everyday scenes that carry the weight of time.

Only when they are seen and cared for do they stand a chance of living on. As the dismantling continues, perhaps one day we will have to walk into a museum just to see the glow of neon. But the moments frozen by the shutter and the weight carried by light and shadow will endure in these images, never to disappear.

We would like to thank @filmlife_ww for participating in this shoot and sharing his heartfelt insights.

What happens when a comic book artist's perspective meets the immediacy of instant film photography?

For this new feature, we sent a Lomo'Instant Automat and a Lomography Soft Cover Photo Album to Émilie Gleason with a simple invitation: make the album her own. Paste in photos, draw around them, write, annotate, collect everyday moments...and let the images become the starting point for a story.

© Photos and illustrations by Émilie Gleason shot on Lomo'Instant Automat

Keeping travel journals to draw and extend her memories, Émilie embraced a new creative exercise: she let instant photography become the thread running through the journal. She captured her baby's first discoveries, preserved the fleeting beauty of a double rainbow, documented her living room before rearranging it, and remembered a marriage proposal that was as unexpected as it was unforgettable. Around each photograph, she added drawings, lists, botanical observations, anecdotes, and reflections.

The result is a journal that feels wonderfully alive: an organized, poetic, unfiltered jumble where every photograph opens the door to a story, and the margins have just as much to say as the images themselves. We spoke with Émilie about her approach to journaling, analogue photography, and her deeply personal way of turning a photo album into a true visual diary. Discover a selection of pages from her journal below, shared here with us.

© Photos and illustrations by Émilie Gleason shot on Lomo'Instant Automat

Welcome to the Magazine! Can you tell us a little about yourself, your relationship with journaling, and analogue photography?

I've been keeping travel journals since I was 18, where I love combining observational and imaginative drawings with anecdotes and personal reflections. My memory is pretty terrible and the way I tell stories is very spontaneous, so these journals are an honest snapshot of who I was in the moment. I love looking back through them because they let me relive those memories almost like a flashback. As for analogue photography, it's always taught me patience: taking the time to think about the moment, the composition, the light, and the subject. It's a process I really enjoy, especially in contrast to digital photography.

What does this journal represent for you?

I'm a new mum, rediscovering the world through my baby's eyes. These first moments are the ones that fade the fastest, so what better way to hold onto them than by keeping a journal?

I also loved the mini format, which gave me the perfect excuse to indulge my second passion after journaling: making lists!

© Photos and illustrations by Émilie Gleason shot on Lomo'Instant Automat

Has instant photography changed the way you document memories in a journal?

Completely. It was such a fun exercise. I usually only take photos of things in museums so I can redraw them later, but this completely changed the way I approached the journal. The photos really gave it structure whether they were spontaneous snapshots (like the double rainbow), taken as a kind of archive (our living room before we rearranged it), or even the failed ones (my self-portrait), which ended up sending me off on all sorts of tangents.

© Photos and illustrations by Émilie Gleason shot on Lomo'Instant Automat

Do you have a favorite page in this journal? If so, what's the story behind it?

That's a tough one! Looking back, June 2026 will always remind me of my marriage proposal. It was completely improvised and wonderfully over the top, appearing on the big screen at a punk concert in front of 1,500 people, including the person I was proposing to, of course. It perfectly captures my constant tug of war between being influenced by old romantic films and seeing marriage as little more than legal protection. It felt like the right moment to mark the occasion.

Another page that's very personal to me is the one where I've listed the biggest laughing fits of my life. I can only recommend making a list of your own. Guaranteed to make you laugh all over again. ;)

© Photos and illustrations by Émilie Gleason shot on Lomo'Instant Automat

A huge thank you to Émilie for opening the pages of her journal and sharing this intimate and deeply creative glimpse into her world with us. Through drawings, instant snapshots, and everyday memories, she reminds us that the most meaningful journals are often the ones that leave room for the unexpected.

If you enjoyed her work, be sure to follow Émilie on Instagram and discover her graphic novels on her website.

The LomoChrome Color '92 ISO 400 120 and the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed ISO 400 120 have been favorites among fans of vintage-inspired film aesthetics. We invited Lin Chao, an urban planner and film photography enthusiast, to share his thoughts on the Sun-kissed edition and how he balances vision and instinct the moment he presses the shutter.

Photos by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

Hi, Lin Chao, welcome to Lomography Magazine! Could you tell our readers a bit about yourself?

My name is Lin Chao. I work as an urban planner, but I’m also a film photography enthusiast. Over the past couple of years, I’ve been focusing more on photography. You could say it’s been a creative gap year in my career.

Photo by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

How did you get started with film photography? You mainly share 120 format work on social media. Do you also shoot other formats?

When I was a kid, compact film cameras were everywhere. But my real introduction to 135 films came in 2012.

I had already been shooting digitally for a few years. Since I was used to the Pentax system and didn’t have a full-frame digital camera, I started experimenting with film bodies like the Pentax MZ-3 and the three FA limited lenses.

That was the real beginning. Later, I moved into 120 format with cameras like the Fuji GA645, Pentax 645NII, Rolleiflex 2.8F, and Fuji GF670. I’ve stuck with 120 ever since. Right now, my main cameras are the Rolleiflex 3.5F and 2.8GX. I occasionally use the Rolleiflex SL66, but I don’t shoot any other formats at the moment.

Photos by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

When you press the shutter, do you usually have a clear image in mind, or do you trust your intuition more?

I usually have a picture in mind before I press the shutter. I can often predict how the final image will turn out. I think that comes with experience. A few thousand meaningful shots are enough to get to that point. Intuition, to me, is an instant reaction formed by habit and aesthetic preference. It comes from both practice and a consistent visual taste.

Photos by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

Your photos always feel quiet and full of light. How did that style develop?

You could say it’s a bit of a “mori girl” vibe, maybe? My wife and I actually connected through photography. In the spring of 2013, I shot a series of her styled in that aesthetic around Liuyun Unit. It unexpectedly gained some traction online. That style stayed with us, and over time more people recognized it. It became something of a signature for both of us.

That Japanese “mori girl” look was quite popular back then, but it was really more about a lifestyle and attitude than an actual connection to forests. The sense of light and quiet atmosphere is simply an extension of that outlook.

Photos by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

You've used quite a few Lomography films before, including Color Negative and LomoChrome Color '92. How would you describe our 120 films in general?

I’ve used Lomography Color Negative ISO 100, 800, and LomoChrome Color '92 ISO 400 quite extensively.

In my experience, Lomography’s 120 films have always offered something a little different. Back in the day, Color Negative 100 was one of my top choices for shooting greenery, and Color Negative 800 was an excellent indoor option. It held its own against high-end 800‑speed competitors.

As for Color ’92, it’s simply the best I’ve used for shooting vintage interiors. With film prices rising across the board, it’s refreshing to see Lomography releasing such distinctive 120 films at this time. It gives photographers more creative options.

Photo by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

What do you think sets the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun‑kissed edition apart? Which scenes did you enjoy the most?

The biggest difference between Color '92 and the Sun‑kissed edition is the color palette. Color '92 leans cooler overall, with magenta hints in the shadows. Sun‑kissed stays consistently warm across the board, indoors or outdoors, at sunrise or sunset. It has a yellowish‑green tint that feels more flattering to Asian skin tones and smoother transitions throughout.

My favorite scene was definitely sunset backlighting. It made the flower fields look incredible.

Photos by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

If you had to describe this film in a few words, what would they be? And if you could pair it with a soundtrack, what song would you choose?

Quiet. Minimal. Scentless.

And the song – The Rose by Aoi Teshima.

Photos by Lin Chao with the LomoChrome Color '92 Sun-kissed 120 ISO 400

Lastly, who would you recommend this film to? Is there any other Lomography film or camera you’d like to try next?

I’d recommend it to anyone who loves minimalism, simple compositions, and modest exposures. As for what’s next, I’m always open to more!

A big thank you to Lin Chao for sharing his work and his thoughts with us. Make sure to follow his page for more of his film photography journey.

We look forward to seeing what quiet, light‑filled moments he’ll capture next with Lomography film.

What happens when three photographers are given the same camera, the same model, and the same location? The shooting setup may be identical, but surely, the way every photographer sees through their lens is different, right?

The Lomography Vienna team explored that idea as Elisa Parrino, Barbara Podstawczynska, and Tony Sotelo went out with their Lomo MC-A cameras in hand to take portraits of model Ginevra Mariottini. Each photographer loaded with a different film stock to interpret the scene: LomoChome Purple, LomoChrome Classicolor, and LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92. Read along to see how each photographer brought their unique visions to life!

Credits: Elisa Parrino using LomoChrome Classicolor, Tony Sotelo using LomoChrome Purple& Barbara Podstawczynska using LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92 | Shot with the Lomo MC-A

One Camera: Shooting Portraits with the Lomo MC-A

Elisa: Shooting with the Lomo MC-A is always quite liberating. The compact size made it really easy for me to move around our model, try different points of view, and get to positions that might have been a bit more challenging or unsafe when using a heavier camera.

Tony: Shooting with the Lomo MC-A was very enjoyable. With most point-and-shoot cameras, your main concern is framing while the camera takes care of the technical decisions. In my case, I used the auto setting as a starting point, but I manually adjusted both the aperture and the focus distance. At times, I wanted the viewer's attention to rest entirely on the model, so I opened up the aperture to deliberately create a shallow depth of field. That level of creative control is something I wouldn’t have had with a fixed-aperture camera.

Credits: Tony Sotelo using LomoChrome Purple, Elisa Parrino using LomoChrome Classicolor& Barbara Podstawczynska using LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92 | Shot with the Lomo MC-A

Barbara: The Lomo MC-A is no Rubik's cube, so I quickly got the hang of operating it. I shot mostly in automatic mode and really appreciated the autofocus – it was both reliable and sharp. Its smooth running was a major plus in such a dynamic setting, with the light shifting fast and quite a lot of passersby moving through the frame.

Elisa: What I like the most about the Lomo MC-A is the versatility of setting that you can switch to quite swiftly. From fully automatic for more spontaneous moments, to semi automatic mood and have some control at my disposal. For example, when the light is quite strong, I like to go up with my apertures and let the shutter speed be determined by the camera.

Tony: Towards the end, I switched to full auto mode and let the camera surprise me. Instead of focusing on technical choices, I concentrated on capturing the emotions of the model and the atmosphere of the location. I enjoyed embracing that unpredictability and seeing how the camera interpreted the final moments of the shoot. Looking back on the developed images, I'm pleased with the results. I think this balance between intentional control and spontaneity gave the series a more genuine and dynamic feel.

Credits: Tony Sotelo using LomoChrome Purple, Elisa Parrino using LomoChrome Classicolor& Barbara Podstawczynska using LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92 | Shot with the Lomo MC-A

Three Visions: Purple vs. Classicolor vs. Color 92

Elisa: I was excited to see the LomoChrome Classicolor shine in this botanical garden. We planned to shoot at sunset to have that glowing warm light and long shadows – it did deliver a great atmosphere. I wanted to convey wonder and dreamy images and I think this film stock did a wonderful job.

Barbara: Having used the LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92 previously, I was able to envision the results in advance. I knew it would match perfectly with the building's beige tones, soften the greens, and handle the strong sunlight well. I knew that this film stock was not about high contrast, but rather playing with light and subtle hues.

Credits: Tony Sotelo using LomoChrome Purple, Barbara Podstawczynska using LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92& Elisa Parrino using LomoChrome Classicolor | Shot with the Lomo MC-A

Tony: One element that strongly influenced my approach was the surrounding greenery. Knowing beforehand that I would be shooting with the LomoChrome Purple, I anticipated that the green tones would shift to purple. This made me reimagine the location as a surreal purple landscape, and details that might not have caught my attention with a different film stock suddenly became the main subjects of my photographs.

Barbara: The LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92's warm, subdued, and slightly faded colors made the photos really stand out. The way this film handles beautiful greens and the light-dappled spaces shows off its powers best.

Elisa: The LomoChrome Classicolor renders the colors of the sunset and the warmth of summer terrifically – the golden light was shining through. It worked especially well with the color of the model’s dress and the location. Everything married harmoniously and I couldn't be happier.

Credits: Barbara Podstawczynska using LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92, Tony Sotelo using LomoChrome Purple& Elisa Parrino using LomoChrome Classicolor | Shot with the Lomo MC-A

The Results: Surprises and Favorites

Barbara: Having had little experience with the Lomo MC-A in the past, I went into this shoot with zero expectations. I walked into it blind, hoping the results would capture the beautiful play of light my eyes were witnessing. In the end, the photos made me more than happy.

Elisa: I enjoyed doing the shoot with two other photographers. I think the challenge of having one model was very fun. Each of us had a different view – even if we were in the same location with the same model, it’s fun to see each person's vision come to life and inspire each other.

Tony: For this project, one of the most interesting aspects was seeing how, despite the three of us photographing the same model in the same location, our images turned out completely different. Each photographer was drawn to different backgrounds, shapes, textures, and details. It was a great reminder that no two people can make the exact same photograph, even when working under the same conditions.

Credits: Tony Sotelo using LomoChrome Purple, Elisa Parrino using LomoChrome Classicolor& Barbara Podstawczynska using LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92 | Shot with the Lomo MC-A

Barbara: I really like the photo in which the model is positioned behind a statue with her face visible. While it is very easy to use statues as the main focus of the image, you are ultimately photographing someone else's artwork. The trick is to use them as a prop and not the primary subject, which I think worked quite well here.

Elisa: I think my favorite shot was Ginevra in the bamboo forest. I love the vibe and the feelings that it evokes. What’s her story? Where is she going? Where is she coming from? I love that I can dream with her. To me, it's quite special when a photo gives you the freedom to imagine wonderful stories.

Tony: This photo is my favorite one. At first glance, it looks like a very simple photograph. There aren’t many elements around, but the more I look at it, the more captivated by the image I feel. Earth and sky coming together, with the human body breaking them apart or merging them. It feels incredibly calm and serene. The purple of the ground makes it feel very dreamy, and I just feel at peace when I look at this photograph. I had a vision when I took it, but the outcome exceeded my intentions.

Credits: Barbara Podstawczynska using LomoChrome Sun-kissed '92, Elisa Parrino using LomoChrome Classicolor& Tony Sotelo using LomoChrome Purple | Shot with the Lomo MC-A

See where your own creative vision takes you and explore more ways of seeing with the Lomo MC-A when you pair it with different Lomography film stocks.

Which photographer’s vision do you relate to the most? Let us know in the comments below!

Felix Kayser is best characterized by his versatility. For the past eleven years, he’s been dedicated to perhaps one of the most beautiful photography genres: portraits. He draws inspiration from all over – from emerging talents like Theo Gosselin to iconic legends like Peter Lindbergh, or the fashion magazine Sibylle, which has been famously referred to as “the Vogue of East Germany”.

This colorful mixture of inspirational sources is also reflected in his portraits. Sometimes in black and white, sometimes in color, often digital but, for the past eight years, increasingly analogue – such as his photo series shot with Lomography Color Negative 120 Film. In this interview, he speaks about his fascination with this medium and what he imagines the future of photography to look like.

© Felix Kayser | Film: Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 100

Hi, Felix, welcome to the Lomography Magazine! Please introduce yourself to our readers.

Hello, Lomography Team! Thank you for the invitation and the opportunity to share my perspective. I’m in my early 40s, and my roots are in Berlin. I grew up in East Berlin, so behind the wall, which continues to influence the way I look at the city of Berlin to this day. Throughout the years, I have also become a Francophile, as my work is often inspired by the aesthetic, the cuisine, and the architecture in France.

How did you get into photography?

Long story short: through Berlin’s gentrification in the 2000s. I wanted to capture the resulting change somehow, and during this time period, I found my way to photography. The shifts across my Kiez (city neighborhood in Berlin/Northern Germany) and the surrounding neighborhoods brought both light and dark, and photography became my way of processing it all. During this time, I saw a lot of historical scenes of everyday life across various photo exhibitions.

Through the perspectives of other photographers, such as Harald Hauswald, Helga Paris or Roger Melis, I then approached photography myself. It was only about eleven years ago that I began taking images of human subjects. During this time, I also discovered my love for manual photography, which I have since integrated into my workflow as the most important stylistic tool. For eight years, I have been loyal only to analogue photography.

© Felix Kayser

Your website quotes Tim Walker: “Only photograph what you love.” To what extent is that achievable as a professional photographer?

You can only really call yourself a professional if you work in a team where everyone is contributing professionally and passionately. On commercial shoots or smaller commissions, I usually guide a specific creative piece of the puzzle, and I like to think that my customers really value my judgment. They trust my photographic eye. For contract work, the customer usually books you based on your style, and that naturally leads to certain expectations about the results.

You will never fully be able to lead this process, simply because there are so many aspects you cannot control. That’s what makes it rewarding, though, as it forces you to communicate, reflect, and evolve with every single project. What counts in the end is that the customer is satisfied and that the images resonate with the intended audience.

© Felix Kayser

Speaking of Tim Walker, do you have any role models in photography?

I already named some of them above. There’s a whole list of photographers that had a big impact on my current work. Definitely Theo Gosselin, Maud Chalard, Pierre Turtaut, and Jean-Philippe Lebee, who really shaped my eye when it comes to mood, spontaneity, and color. But also photographers from East Germany, such as Ute Mahler and Sibylle Bergemann: back in the day, they produced a lot of iconic and, in their own way, timeless images for the so-called East German Vogue “Sibylle” and fundamentally influenced contemporary photography.

Robert Lebeck and Peter Lindbergh’s treatment of top models during their peak time is proof of how various styles can impact generations of photographers. And yet, I’m constantly amazed to see how many young people are reinventing classical photography, infusing it with a fresh zeitgeist.

“...speaking of imperfect shots: it is those in particular that often stand out, as they are able to better translate the feel of specific moments.”

Considering that you specialize in portrait photography: how would you characterize a good portrait?

First of all: there is no good or bad! It’s just that some portraits affect us more than others. But it’s definitely about the communication that occurs between the protagonist and me. I don’t see much value in merely enforcing my own perspective. That might seem rather intangible to others. But it’s only through communicating and expressing ideas and moods that thoughts can truly be conveyed. This process creates opportunities where you can truly capture light, shadows, environments and outfits in an intriguing and profound way.

Of course, the light conditions are just half the story, and it should be neither too bright nor too dark. Nevertheless, there are no rigid rules, not even in that case. The boundaries of optical physics should be pushed in photography, and can even be broken every once in a while. And speaking of imperfect shots: it is those in particular that often stand out, as they are able to better translate the feel of specific moments.

© Felix Kayser | Film: Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 100

What do your shootings normally look like? What’s important to you?

Also in this case, communication is essential right from the beginning. Everything should be addressed directly and openly: moods, wishes, concerns, and ideas. And if possible, that process shouldn’t be stressful. It’s essential to agree on outfits, location, plan B, and a good gut feeling at all times. In bigger teams, this becomes even more important, as you can never guess someone else’s thoughts. If all of that has been settled, from then onwards it’s just a matter of the right lighting. I prefer natural light whenever possible. Good studio lighting takes a serious budget and logistics, which isn't always feasible.

If you had to decide, would you prefer, digital or analogue photography?

That question is always hard! To be honest, when the sun is out, I’ll happily turn to analogue. If the lighting is challenging, definitely digital.

You’ve already used 120 films by Lomography multiple times. What was your experience?

Yes, a while ago I discovered the Color Negative ISO 100, 400, and 800 films, and since then I always keep some in my fridge. Thanks to the Lomo Community, I read some reviews and saw reference photos. I thought the blues were intriguing and the Color Negative ISO 400 clearly impressed me with its clean look. You can’t really go wrong with that.

© Felix Kayser

Which Lomography product would you like to test in the future?

The LomoChrome Color ’92 ISO 400 in medium format is definitely at the top of my list. Particularly because it represents a look from a time when I was a child. My first idea would be to capture some sort of vintage fashion from that time in a photo series.

We’re living in a time of both analogue-hype and artificial intelligence. What do you wish for the future of photography?

Well, it’s certainly not going to die! I just hope it remains a viable part of the creative industry as a whole, rather than being pushed purely into fine art. Analogue photography is already an expensive endeavor today, so I hope it remains financially possible for young photographers to shoot film and print on paper. Luckily, there are still passionate camera makers out there who will continue releasing new products.

© Felix Kayser | Film: Lomography Color Negative 120 ISO 400

Is there anything else you’d like to share with the Community?

Just do it and remain optimistic! Visit exhibitions more often or watch independent films – the most important thing is to get away from digital channels and algorithm-based bubbles every once in a while.

Thank you very much for this nice interview, Felix!

If you’d like to see more of Felix and his work, follow him on Instagram and visit his website.

Balancing photography, video, and visual experimentation, Emma Cortijo continues to shape a world that is both intuitive and deeply evocative, driven by music, movement, and a constant desire to capture the moment. Since our last conversation, her creative vision has evolved toward more spontaneous imagery, with digital photography and video now playing central roles, while never completely letting go of the unique charm of film.

In this new interview, Emma reflects on her experience with the Joseph Petzval 27 mm f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens, which she tested outdoors and in low-light conditions, including during a live performance by musical artist Enola Cox. Captivated by its signature swirling bokeh and distinctive rendering, she shares how the lens encouraged her to explore more organic imagery.

Credits: Emma Cortijo | With the Joseph Petzval 27 f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Hello, Emma, we're delighted to have you back in the Magazine! Since your last interview with us, how has your way of working evolved?

Hello! The feeling is mutual. I think the biggest change is that I've stepped away from film photography a little. I've been coming back to it recently just for the pleasure of it, but these days I'm much more focused on digital and video, capturing moments and movement in a very spontaneous way.

What inspires you the most at the moment, beyond photography and filmmaking?

Music has always been my biggest source of inspiration. I've always loved it. I just didn't choose that path professionally, but it still drives me. Certain songs or lyrics immediately spark visual ideas and make me imagine images I want to create. It's a real creative engine for me. I'm also a huge fan of playlists, and I sometimes make them to help immerse people even more deeply in a project I'm presenting.

Credits: Emma Cortijo | With the Joseph Petzval 27 f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Has there been a particular moment or project that marked a turning point in your career?

There have been quite a few. Sometimes it's photographing someone I really admire, shooting in an iconic concert venue, or completing a personal project I'm especially proud of. But what means the most to me is having the freedom to experiment with whatever I want, and being able to make a living from it over the past few years.

Can you tell us about your experience with the Petzval lens? In what situations did you use it, and what did you choose to shoot?

I first tested it outdoors in daylight, then I wanted to see what the swirling bokeh would look like in low light, and I absolutely loved it. I ended up using it again to create visuals with a more cinematic feel for video content.

What were your first impressions when you started using it?

It took me a little while to get used to it because I'd become so accustomed to modern lenses that manual focusing didn't feel as natural anymore. But I got the hang of it pretty quickly. Even in situations with a lot of movement, where the focus wasn't always perfect, that imperfection actually became part of its charm.

Video 1

Were there any particular moments, whether because of the light, the atmosphere, or the subject, when you felt the lens really showed its full potential?

I think I prefer using it in low light, or with a background that's rich in detail. Whether it's points of light in the distance or a scene with lots of visual elements, that's when you really start to appreciate the bokeh effect.

How did the lens perform with your camera?

It was a great match for my Nikon ZR. I hadn't used a lens like this on it before, and it offers a completely different look compared to modern lenses. I think it's a really interesting option depending on the kind of project I want to create.

Credits: Emma Cortijo | With the Joseph Petzval 27 f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Did features like the adjustable bokeh settings, focus-coupled design, or follow focus compatibility influence the way you framed your shots?

I think it made me want to embrace shots that felt more organic and less perfectly stable. Without this lens, I usually rely on my camera's built-in stabilization, which gives me really clean footage and is incredibly practical. With the Petzval, I enjoyed seeing what happened when I let movement become part of the image.

Was there a particular shot or image from this shoot that stood out to you?

The moment on stage with Enola Cox, opening for Helena at the Zénith de Paris, with all the stage lights on. I absolutely love those images.

Credits: Emma Cortijo | With the Joseph Petzval 27 f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

What kind of projects do you see yourself using this lens for in the future? Which creative worlds do you think it suits best?

I'd definitely use it for music videos. I haven't had the opportunity yet, but maybe that will happen later this year!

Video 2

Credits: Emma Cortijo | With the Joseph Petzval 27 f/1.7 Focus-Coupled Bokeh Control Art Lens

Finally, what advice would you give to a photographer or filmmaker using this lens for the first time?

Be a little patient at first, and try it in different situations before using it on a major project. That way, you'll have time to understand what makes it unique and learn how to get the best out of it.

A big thank you to Emma for taking the time to answer our questions. To discover more of her work, be sure to follow her on Instagram and visit her website.

In search of the lush green vitality of midsummer and a touch of nostalgic early-2000s freshness, LomoAmiga Mina Cho headed to Yeouido Saetgang Ecological Park in Seoul with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor.

Combining built-in color gel flash filters, vertical framing, soap bubbles, and creative lighting, a fantastical summer scene was brought to life within the half-frame format. Set against a backdrop of retro music, check out her honest and charming story about this location shoot and the liberating perspective that analogue photography brings.

© Mina Cho | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor | Model: Sowon

Hello, Mina! Great to see you again. Could you please introduce yourself?

Hello! It’s great to connect with you again after a while. I’m Mina Cho, a photographer who creates various works through the medium of film, and a fellow LomoAmiga.

How did you get started with analogue film photography? And what does film mean to you as a medium?

I began working seriously with film after getting married in 2020. Before that, it was just a hobby I loved in the past, but I hadn't been able to pick up a camera easily because life was so busy. People often say that getting married means cutting back on the hobbies you love, but in my case, it was the exact opposite thanks to my husband, who is very clear about what he wants to do! (Laughs) For me, film is something that evokes a sense of nostalgia for my childhood in the 1990s.

© Mina Cho | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor | Model: Sowon

Even the somewhat cumbersome process – from the limited number of shots that forces you to think deeply right before pressing the shutter, to the post-processing that continues after shooting – feels incredibly charming to me. I also love the unexpected variables and expressive qualities that result differently every time, depending on the film type, shooting environment, and the photographer’s approach.

Above all, the most attractive point is that you can’t see the results immediately on site. It prevents me from getting trapped in the frame of ‘my photos’ and allows me to capture the world from a richer, freer perspective.

Did you have any prior experience with the half-frame format? What was your first impression when you saw the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera?

I had previously used various half-frame cameras, such as the Olympus Pen EE series, the Kyocera Yashica Samurai series, and Lomography’s Half-Frame Lomourette. Since older models tend to be small and compact, their viewfinders were also small, which made the view feel a bit cramped. On the other hand, this Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Camera features a large, clear viewfinder, making it very comfortable on the eyes with no sense of restriction when shooting.

© Mina Cho | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor | Model: Sowon

Please tell us about your experience shooting with this camera. Where did you go, and what did you capture?

I went on a shoot to Yeouido Saetgang Ecological Park. Since it was during the monsoon season and securing natural light could have been difficult, I packed portable lighting along with a bag full of cute props. Working with Sowon, a professional model, we captured the vibrant green vitality and humidity unique to midsummer right inside the frame.

The Half-Frame Simple Use Camera is reloadable, features a built-in flash with interchangeable color gel filters, and is easy to operate, as its name suggests. Which feature did you like the most? Or what element gave you new creative inspiration?

Just as its name suggests, it felt like a Simple Use camera optimized for user convenience. My favorite feature was undoubtedly the wide, open viewfinder, and I was also impressed by how stable the grip felt despite it being a plastic camera.

© Mina Cho | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor | Model: Sowon

It was also super fun to combine the three color gel filters attached to the built-in flash right on the spot to add color to the light. Above all, while most half-frame cameras default to a landscape orientation, I found it very appealing that this camera is optimized for a portrait orientation.

“My favorite feature was undoubtedly the wide, open viewfinder, and I was also impressed by how stable the grip felt despite it being a plastic camera.”

Is there a particular photo among those shot with this camera that stands out in your memory? Could you share the behind-the-scenes story for that shot?

(First) The frame where I used acrylic sheets and water to create a sense of space stands out to me. I wanted to give a unique sense of three-dimensionality and depth to the camera's output.

© Mina Cho | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor | Model: Sowon

(Second) There is also a shot taken by combining soap bubbles and lighting. We were able to complete it thanks to Sowon bringing her own bubble gun. To get the shot we wanted, we blew a huge number of bubbles, but every time we pressed the bubble gun button, a children’s cartoon song played out loud, which was a little embarrassing... (Laughs). Thanks to that, I had a really fun time working with Sowon.

Was there any music that came to mind while shooting with the half-frame camera? If you could express your experience with this camera as a single song, what would it be?

When I look at Sowon, she reminds me of a film camera – retro, yet somehow evoking the fresh atmosphere of the early 2000s. So there was a song I had in mind beforehand: Lalala, It’s Love! by The Melody, well known as the original soundtrack from the drama Coffee Prince.

Holding a film camera while thinking of this song naturally brought back nostalgic feelings and school-day memories from that era. I wanted to bring out a look somewhere between a young girl and an adult by combining Sowon's retro mood with playful, child-like props.

© Mina Cho | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor | Model: Sowon

In half-frame photography, two adjacent photos often come together to tell a single story. What did you keep in mind when connecting the model's expressions or movements?

Since two shots combine to form one frame, I try to avoid compositions where both sides are tightly packed only with the subject. For instance, if I capture the subject on the left side in one frame, I might place them in the center or on the right in the next shot to create a natural flow of sight lines.

If one side focuses on the upper body, the other side might capture the full body; or if both are upper-body shots, I direct completely different poses. If one side emphasizes a prop, I might focus purely on the person on the other side. In this way, I pay close attention to combining static and dynamic flows between the shots.

© Mina Cho | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor | Model: Sowon

Do you have any personal shooting tips to get the most out of the Half-Frame Simple Use Camera?

First off, since the aperture isn't very bright, I recommend shooting under bright natural light or in spaces with sufficient artificial light. Also, as a fixed-focus camera at 0.6 m, you would normally stick to this distance, but framing within 0.6 m can sometimes be a fun experiment. By intentionally blurring specific areas, you can create a unique mood that can only be felt through film.

For the color gel filters on the flash, if you figure out in advance which color combinations produce which tones, you'll be able to achieve much higher quality results. Finally, if you use the nature of half-frame photography – where two shots connect – as your own storytelling or staging tool, you’ll find handling this camera to be a truly enjoyable experience.

Where would you like to travel next with this camera?

Since I captured the green vitality of summer in this project, next time I’d love to capture a blue-toned summer featuring the deep blue sea or glistening watersides. Of course, anywhere with plenty of natural light would be wonderful. And if Lomography happens to release a dedicated underwater case for this model, I’d love to challenge myself with unique underwater staging using the half-frame format.

Thank you to Mina for testing the Half-Frame Simple Use Reloadable Camera and sharing her special shooting experience and tips. Follow Mina's Instagram page to enjoy more of her emotional work.

Why not head out on your summer vacation with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Classicolor? You’ll be able to vividly capture the unadorned, fleeting moments of life within the half-frame format.
