In this edition of A Day With, we invite you into the unique world and vibrant everyday life of LomoAmiga Yung. A marketer and artist who has long embraced analogue photography, Yung recently brought the Lomo’Instant Automat to the opening of a colleague's solo exhibition. What special moments did she capture on instant film? Discover her heartfelt photographs and stories through this feature.

© Yung | Lomo’Instant Automat

> Hello! I'm Yung, a marketer and artist with a passion for music, travel, and analogue photography. Alongside writing and giving talks, I run a multidisciplinary creative community, and a creative studio that operates as a freelance collective. While I often work independently as a solo creator, I'm also fortunate to collaborate with many talented people as part of a team.

© Yung | Lomo’Instant Automat

> I’ve loved cameras for as long as I can remember and have been collecting them since my teenage years. I especially enjoy using several Lomography cameras, and I also own a variety of Polaroid models. I was delighted to have the chance to try the Lomo’Instant Automatfor the first time, and it became even more enjoyable once I started shooting with it. I love that you can experiment with different lens attachments and even create multiple exposures within an instant camera.

© Yung | Lomo’Instant Automat

> Since I don’t have a fixed commute and can work from anywhere, the places and scenes that fill my days are always changing. Last Friday, one of our crew members opened their first solo exhibition in Incheon, so a few of us who were available went along to celebrate. It was also my first time taking the Lomo’Instant Automat out for a spin, and I used it to capture photos of my friends throughout the day.

> Taking pictures on the way there, over a meal, and while celebrating the exhibition together made the whole experience even more enjoyable.

© Yung | Lomo’Instant Automat

> I experimented with the fisheye, close-up, and wide-angle lens attachments. Switching among them was a lot of fun, but I also liked that the camera can capture a wider view without an attachment, and I was especially pleased with its natural colors. It also comes with a remote control cleverly designed to resemble a lens cap, which made taking group photos together incredibly easy. It’s the perfect camera for capturing memories with friends!

© Yung | Lomo’Instant Automat

> Next time, I'd love to experiment more with the camera by exploring its multiple exposure feature. I also want to photograph my own space indoors, and since the camera has a small selfie mirror on the front, it's perfect for self-portraits, too, which I'm excited to try. I hope to keep capturing the little moments that make everyday life sparkle.

© Yung | Lomo’Instant Automat

In frame: Hyeyun Jung, Seulgi Lee, Moyeon Song, Jaehyung Park, Jaeseong Park, Dayeon Lee

What did you think of LomoAmiga Yung's day captured with the Lomo'Instant Automat? We hope the special moments seen through her lens brought a little inspiration and excitement to your own everyday life. If you'd like to see more of her work and daily adventures, be sure to visit her Instagram.

You can explore more stories from our A Day With series in the Magazine.

Our Magazine series, Creators in Focus, highlights experimental minds around the world who are pushing boundaries, and finding new ways to live life more analogue.

In the creative universe of Hong Kong-based artist Tobie Tse, hand-stitched tapestries are brought to life through a combination of illustrations, crochet, and video editing. As a multimedia creator, Tobie believes in the importance of exploration and allows experimentation to guide her practice across these different forms of art. Come along as we get a closer look at Tobie’s artworks and the creative process behind them.

Credits: Tobie Tse

Welcome to the Lomography Magazine, Tobie! For our readers who are meeting you for the first time, could you share a little bit about yourself and what you do?

Hi, thank you for having me! I'm a multimedia creator based in Hong Kong, mainly working at the intersection of fiber arts and technology.

Has creativity always been a part of your life? Tell us how and when you first got into visual art.

Yes, absolutely. I drew a lot as a child, which was my first real creative outlet, and continued exploring other forms as I got older. I also fell in love with cinema around the age of fifteen, and made lots of silly short films with friends at school.

How would you describe your creative style? Are there any recurring themes, processes, or elements that you find yourself drawn to?

I’m quite sentimental and nostalgic. A lot of what I create is rooted in personal experience, so my work tends to reflect where I am emotionally at any given moment. I also keep returning to themes and motifs that feel timeless – things that feel universally relatable. Visually, I’m drawn to nature for both form and color: flowers, animals, plants, and earthy tones are recurring influences in my work.

Credits: Tobie Tse

Your practice spans across different forms of expression – illustration, graphic design, animation, and even textile art like crochet. How important do you think is exploration and experimentation in growing as an artist?

[It is] so important to me. I’m highly self-critical, and I often feel frustrated with what I make – at times to the point of wanting to abandon the work entirely. What’s helped me push through the creative block is shifting to, and exploring, other mediums. This creates room to experiment, and it gives me a way to refine my niche over time.

I never would have imagined combining crochet and animation without allowing myself that space for exploration. What makes these pieces so process-visible is how fully they reveal my workflow. I’m not just combining crochet with animation; I’m bringing together the whole chain of my practice – drawing/illustration, video editing, textile craft – into one unified process. The resulting work reads as a coherent reflection of my practice: the skills I’ve developed and the way I integrate them.

As a multimedia creator, how does each medium you work with shape the way you communicate your ideas? Is there a particular form of art that feels most meaningful to you?

Film and moving images will always feel closest to me as a creative form. I find storytelling comes most naturally through movement – refined by sound and pacing. In my own practice, still forms can feel limiting, but motion opens things up and makes the work more expansive and interesting.

Video 1

Credits: Tobie Tse

Credits: Tobie Tse

You recently created crochet animations of lyric teasers for Olivia Rodrigo. What was the experience like and could you share a bit about your technical process in making these?

The experience was extraordinary! Such opportunities are rare, and I am so grateful to Olivia and her team for making it possible.

The process began with analogue methods. I considered the visual language appropriate to the lyrics and hand-drew the initial frames. These drawings were then translated into digital crochet patterns, which I used to crochet the “blank” frames. From there, I generated the intermediary frames – based on frame-by-frame inbetweening – before digitally stitching together the individual cells of the crochet grid to produce motion. For the lyrics, I referenced archival sources of vintage cross-stitch and filet lace patterns to inform the typographic style. Once the frames were ready, I exported individually and assembled them into the stop-motion sequence.

“...creative agency is about the cycle of error, recalibration, learning from others, and the final ‘product’ of a piece should bear traces of this process. The act of making art is something deeply and fundamentally human...”

When and how did you discover crochet animation?

After crocheting for about four years, I only discovered crochet animation in May this year. This format is still new to me, and I’m excited to explore its possibilities further.

My initial inspiration came from a desire to return to film and to create artwork incorporating motion. While working on garments that used filet crochet, I became interested in combining these interests into a single practice.

Credits: Tobie Tse

Aside from crochet animations, you also work with incorporating illustrations to videos. What do you like most about working with mixed media and blending handmade elements with digital processes?

I have two answers to this, and one perhaps too honest! The first is the novelty of mixed media. It's a significant trend at the moment, and crochet is similarly having a moment. Combining these forms struck me as visually compelling and new – two disciplines I hadn't yet seen, brought together in this particular way. I also think that in an age dominated by CGI animation and increasingly accessible 3D modelling software, there is something quite beautiful in the small imperfections that tangible materials in animation inevitably carries.

My second answer: I don’t think I’m exceptional in any one discipline. I think I’m an okay crochet artist, an okay film editor, an okay illustrator. Whether my work within any one medium is remarkable enough on its own, I’m not sure, but combined, I think they amount to something greater and more unique.

With AI-generated art becoming more common these days, what do you think keeps handmade art meaningful and irreplaceable?

To me, generative AI imagery presents little that is technically or aesthetically remarkable. I feel it negates the phenomenological core and essence of art-making completely; creative agency is about the cycle of error, recalibration, learning from others, and the final ‘product’ of a piece should bear traces of this process. The act of making art is something deeply and fundamentally human, and I think people who value creative practice beyond its surface appeal will always have an appreciation for handmade work.

Credits: Tobie Tse

Is there a creative philosophy or belief that guides your practice – something you hope other creators can take with them?

Be patient and be kind to yourself. I’ve tried so many visual art forms – photography, film, painting, printmaking – I know all the more that it takes a while to find your niche.

Lastly, what’s next for you? Are there any upcoming projects or ideas that you’re excited to explore?

The stop motion and crochet hybrid I have been developing feels distinctive, and I am eager to push it further – perhaps toward a short film rendered entirely through filet crochet. I’m also keen to create more with my friends in adjacent creative fields, maybe working towards a collective project that showcases our own relevant disciplines!

Video 2

Credits: Tobie Tse

Analogue endures through material processes, lived rhythms, and practices that ask us to slow down. Creators in Focus follows these sensibilities beyond photography, through voices like Tobie's that keep analogue alive across disciplines.

Want to see Tobie's upcoming projects and more? Explore her art and follow her creative journey by checking out her Instagram page.

Nur Aishah Kenton has a gift for translating intimate connections directly onto film. By weaving her photographs into series, she creates an inner dynamic and poetry that elevates the personal into the universal. In this interview, she shares her conceptual and practical process while reflecting on the role of analogue photography today.

© Nur Aishah Kenton | From the series To Whom It May Concern

Hi, Aishah, and welcome to Lomography Magazine. Could you please introduce yourself to our Community and say a few words about your relationship with analogue photography?

Hello! My name is Nur Aishah Kenton. I am an artist and photographer based in Naarm/Melbourne, Australia. My practice explores how photography, particularly analogue photography, can be used to investigate the world around me and the relationships that shape it. I often work collaboratively, using photography as a means of connection, dialogue, and shared authorship.

In your portfolio, you describe your practice as ‘between life and art, between photography and love’. Those intimate, close moments captured on film are especially visible in your series, Orchid and To Whom It May Concern. Please say a few words about these projects and your work with film photography in this context.

Photography has always come from a deeply personal place for me. I don't see a distinction between my life and my art, my practice is shaped by my relationships and lived experiences, and much of what motivates me comes directly from the world around me.

To Whom It May Concern was my first major body of work, and my graduating series from university. Through a series of photographs and three artist books, it explored my relationship with my partner. Looking back, I can see how pivotal the project was in helping me find my voice as an artist. It introduced ideas that continue to shape my practice today, particularly an interest in bringing intimate, private experiences into the public realm through photography.

© Nur Aishah Kenton | From the series Orchid

Nearly eight years later, Orchid revisits many of those same questions, but through a different relationship. Instead of focusing on my partner, the work centers on my mother. Photography becomes both a therapeutic and collaborative process, one that allows us to reconnect, reflect on our shared history, and navigate the complexities of family, memory, and identity together. While the subject has shifted, the underlying motivations remain the same: using photography to better understand the people closest to me and the relationships that have shaped who I am.

Why do you consistently choose analogue over digital, and how does it influence your storytelling?

I began my artistic practice working with analogue photography, and I'm incredibly grateful that it became the foundation of how I make images. It continues to shape not only my process, but also the way I think about photography and collaboration.

“I think there's something about the materiality and slower pace of analogue photography that continues to resonate, especially in a time when we're constantly surrounded by digital images.”

Returning to analogue photography time and again encourages me to be fully present with the people I photograph. Without the ability to immediately review an image on the back of a camera, my attention remains on the person in front of me rather than the photograph itself. That slower, more intentional process fosters trust, conversation, and genuine connection.

Many of the topics you work with seem to stem from your close environment and personal experiences. How do you find your inspiration, and what does your photographic process look like?

A lot of my inspiration comes from photography itself, but just as much of it comes from being in the world. Outside of my practice, I work as an arts educator and arts worker, and I feel incredibly fortunate that these roles allow me to spend time with people from many different backgrounds and communities. Those conversations, encounters, and relationships continually shape the way I think about photography and often become the starting point for new work.

© Nur Aishah Kenton | From the series Orchid

I'm also an avid reader, particularly of non-fiction and memoir. I'm drawn to the ways people tell stories about their lives, and I often find myself inspired by the intimacy, vulnerability, and complexity that memoirs can hold.

My photographic process almost always begins with listening and with a sense of enquiry. Often it emerges from something I've experienced personally or a question that I can't quite let go of. Rather than beginning with a fully formed concept or carefully planning a project, I usually start by photographing. Making photographs is how I think through an idea.

It is only afterwards when I'm editing, sequencing, and spending time with the images that I begin to understand what I have been drawn to. In many ways, the photographs lead me to the work, rather than the other way around.

On the technical side, what methods and tools do you usually use in film photography, and are they accessible to beginners?

I have dyscalculia, which affects the way I engage with numbers and mathematics, so I've naturally developed a photographic process that isn't overly technical. Instead, I try to keep my workflow as simple and intuitive as possible, allowing me to focus on the relationships I'm building and the photographs I'm making rather than the equipment itself.

“I don't see a distinction between my life and my art...and much of what motivates me comes directly from the world around me.”

When I first started photographing, I was eager to experiment with as many film cameras as I could. While that period of exploration was valuable, I eventually realized that constantly changing cameras wasn't necessarily helping my practice. These days, I work primarily with just two film cameras, and I know them well. Having a simple, familiar kit allows me to concentrate on the people I'm photographing rather than the mechanics of the camera.

© Nur Aishah Kenton | From the series Orchid

I also develop a large part of my process after making the photographs. I scan my own negatives, which has become a therapeutic part of my practice. I enjoy the slower pace of sitting with each image as it emerges, and scanning my own film also gives me greater control over the final look of my photographs.

For me, film photography isn't about having the most technical setup or the newest equipment. It's about finding a process that feels sustainable, intentional, and allows you to stay connected to the photographs you're making.

What advice would you give to someone who wants to start shooting film and use it as a means of artistic expression?

My biggest piece of advice is simply to photograph. If you have an idea, don't wait until it feels fully formed, start by making photographs. Beginning is often the hardest part, but once you've taken that first image, the process has a way of unfolding naturally.

I also can't stress enough how important it is to surround yourself with people who inspire you and who you trust to look at your work. Photography can sometimes feel like an isolating medium, but it doesn't have to be. Some of the most meaningful moments in my practice have come through conversations with friends, mentors, and collaborators who have challenged and encouraged me.

Don't be afraid to reach out to artists whose work you admire, share your photographs with others, and collaborate with friends.

As a practicing analogue photographer from the younger generation, what have you observed about the way film photography is currently used and celebrated? Are there any changes you would like to see in this field?

It's been wonderful to see so many people returning to film photography and embracing it in different ways, whether that's documenting their everyday lives, experimenting creatively, or developing a long term artistic practice. I think there's something about the materiality and slower pace of analogue photography that continues to resonate, especially in a time when we're constantly surrounded by digital images.

© Nur Aishah Kenton | From left, photographs from the series Orchid and To Whom It May Concern

Living and working in Naarm/Melbourne, I feel incredibly fortunate to have access to such a strong analogue photography community. There are multiple labs where I can develop film, artists who continue to champion the medium, and opportunities to learn from one another. That kind of infrastructure and community makes a huge difference in supporting people who are interested in analogue photography.

One thing I would love to see more of is greater accessibility. Film photography can be an expensive medium to sustain, and that financial barrier can prevent many people from engaging with it. I'd also like to see more opportunities for knowledge-sharing across generations.

Thank you, Nur Aishah, for sharing with us the backstage of your inspiring practice. If you are curious about Nur Aishah's ongoing photography work, check out her Instagram @aishah_k and website.

https://www.lomography.com/magazine/3592.content:
What are you most passionate about? We know you love film, but what’s the other thing that keeps you inspired? Here at Lomography, we’re united by our love for film, but we’re just as excited to discover everyone’s passions beyond photography. Shot With Love invites you to shoot that other hobby, interest, or obsession – and weave them into the world of analogue!

Community member Julian Garcia (@juliangarcia) recently took us on a tour around Buenos Aires through a travel guide interview. Now, he's back to share more of his analogue photography as he looks back on his long-time passion for music and delves into what makes capturing it on film so special.

  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/28667757)
  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29515620)
  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29605142)

Credits: juliangarcia

The following words are written by Julian:

Music has been a part of my life for much longer than photography. For around ten years, I played music with friends and was in a band myself, so I spent a lot of time in rehearsal rooms and venues. When I started taking photographs, it seemed natural to eventually bring a camera into that world. For the first few years, though, I mostly avoided photographing shows.

These places were usually dark, crowded and not particularly friendly to an old film camera, and I did not really want to spend film on photographs that I was not sure I could expose properly. Eventually, I decided to try anyway. One of the first times I brought a camera to a show, I took one of my favourite photographs just before the performance. That was enough to make me want to keep trying.

[](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/28392562)

Credits: juliangarcia

I started with a fast 50 mm lens and simply worked with the available light. I quickly found out that 400 ISO was often not enough for very dim interiors, so I started pushing film, especially black and white stocks, usually +2 (1600 ISO) or +3 (3200 ISO). Since I was shooting so much black and white film, I eventually started developing it at home. This was partly a way to reduce the cost, but I quickly became very interested in the process itself.

There is a very specific moment when developing a roll that I really enjoy: opening the tank after fixing the film and seeing the negatives for the first time. The combination of unpredictable stage lighting and film makes every roll slightly more uncertain, and that is a big part of the appeal for me.

  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29625035)
  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29752520)
  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29752515)
  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29515618)

Credits: juliangarcia

Photographing live music is very different from photographing still scenes. Everything is moving, the light is constantly changing, and there is very little time to think about an image. Grain, blur, imperfect focus and strange exposure can all become part of the photograph. I find that these pictures often convey much more emotion, although I am still not completely sure why. The faces are often reduced to shadows or partly disappear into the light. This creates a certain distance from the subject, and I think it leaves more room for the viewer to react to the image rather than simply reading the expression of the person in it.

  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/28828431)
  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29398643)
  • [](https://www.lomography.com/homes/juliangarcia/photos/29310430)

Credits: juliangarcia

Later, I bought a flash, mainly so I could get some more straightforward photographs of the band. These pictures are useful as a record, and I still enjoy them, but they usually feel less interesting to me than the photographs made entirely with the stage light.

I think this is where analogue photography fits naturally with live music for me. The conditions are unpredictable, the results are not immediate, and some of the best images only reveal themselves later.

Check out Julian's other music-related shots and more by following his LomoHome and Instagram. Explore our Shot With Love series and find more passions shared by other Community members here.

What other passions have you combined with analogue photography? We'd love to hear from you – tell us your story and email [[email protected]](https://www.lomography.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#610c0006001b080f044c1214030c081212080e0f210d0e0c0e0613001109184f020e0c) with the subject line: Shot With Love.

Earlier this year, Marc Haeffner took our Berlin Kino B&W 35 mm ISO 400 Film back to its namesake and spoke about his experience in an inspiring interview. A few weeks later, he came back with an exciting pitch for a summer series on pocket film, and we were more than happy to be involved in it! We sent him a Lomomatic 110 Camera and some of our 110 films so he could experiment with this format.

True to his creative spirit, Marc decided to split his introduction to pocket photography into two parts, exploring two completely different concepts on the same camera (and keeping us on the edge of our seats for the results). In this first feature, Marc shares the motivation behind his project and what continues to fascinate him about 110 film. He takes us along on his initial shoot and offers a glimpse into the experiences that gave this article its title.

© Marc Haeffner | Shot with the Lomomatic 110&LomoChrome Classicolor 110 ISO 200

> I’m Marc Haeffner, I’ve been living in Berlin for almost four years, and I work as a photographer. Fashion, art, events, portraits, editorials, or documentary photography, that’s where you’ll find me. Documentary is my favorite. I love documenting my surroundings, my life, my routines, and the people I care about. I enjoy building that personal archive and showing everyday life.

> I'm happy to be back here with my friends at Lomography, especially with the chance to talk about one of my favorite subjects: home.

© Marc Haeffner | Shot with the Lomomatic 110&LomoChrome Classicolor 110 ISO 200

> Living in a city other than the one where you grew up in has its pros and cons. There’s no need to get into that now, but I do want to highlight the value of every moment you get to go back home, spend time with your family and friends, and breathe the air you instantly recognize as home. In my case, that’s the Mediterranean air of Barcelona.

> I have to admit that I wasn’t familiar with the 110 format, and I had never used a pocket camera before. I was shocked by how different the experience is. You stop thinking about focusing, metering, or calculating.

> You simply shoot on instinct and trust the camera to do the work and give you an honest image. I guess that even though I've been shooting analogue for a long time now, I've always used fully manual, medium format cameras that take time to handle, so this felt like a relief.

© Marc Haeffner | Shot with the Lomomatic 110&LomoChrome Classicolor 110 ISO 200

> I haven’t tried any other 110 cameras, only the Lomography Lomomatic 110. One of the things I appreciated most was how much confidence you can place in it. It always finds a way to capture the image and gives you something that feels either sharp or poetic. That’s how I experienced the 110 camera.

“The Lomomatic 110 feels like a little piece of jewelry on your wrist. It has a satisfying weight and feels completely effortless to use.”

> Living abroad makes weekends back home feel even more special, and this time I brought my Lomomatic 110 in my pocket.

> The grain and the spontaneous moments we used to capture as kids with our little cameras, the feeling of not being afraid and simply pressing the shutter to capture life as it is. Returning to this world brought me home, literally and figuratively.

© Marc Haeffner | Shot with the Lomomatic 110&LomoChrome Classicolor 110 ISO 200

> I let the Mediterranean sun, the salt, and the colors flow through the camera, and everything happened naturally. Enjoying the moment with family and friends, enjoying good food, and embracing the feeling of not caring about anything else. The Lomomatic 110 feels like a little piece of jewelry on your wrist. It has a satisfying weight and feels completely effortless to use.

> Important tip, though!Don't forget to adjust the focus distance selector before every shot, or your photos might turn out a little blurry – or, forget it – happy accidents exist. That actually happened to me, but you know what? I decided to embrace the format, the colors, and the special, honest way this camera captures reality.

© Marc Haeffner | Shot with the Lomomatic 110&LomoChrome Classicolor 110 ISO 200

The second part of Marc's experience with the 110 camera will be published soon, so stay tuned!

We'd like to thank Marc for deciding to brave pocket film photography with our Lomomatic 110, and for letting us be part of that journey! For more of his work, make sure to check out @marchaeffner and @expandedarchive on Instagram, as well as his website.

Peter Seljan is living proof that even with a busy 9-5 job, you can still master street photography. After an eye surgery prompted him to pick up the camera, he never looked back. For Peter, every step of shooting analogue photos is sacred, and he treasures every negative he shoots. He recently captured the people and the vibrant spirit of Budapest using Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

Hi, Peter! Welcome to the Lomography Magazine. We are happy to have you! Could you please introduce yourself to our readers?

Thank you very much for having me. My name is Peter Seljan, and I’m from Budapest, Hungary. Photography has become one of my biggest passions. I started taking photos several years ago, after having LASIK surgery. I was so happy to finally have good eyesight that I created an Instagram account, bought my first camera – a DSLR – in 2019, and started with travel photography in my free time.

Eventually, I switched to analogue street photography. I'm not a professional photographer, so most of the time I'm figuring things out as I go. Every roll of film and every photograph feels like an opportunity to learn something new, and that's what I enjoy most about shooting film.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

From what we can see, you picked up your first analogue camera quite recently. What made you start using this medium?

That is correct. Analogue photography is still relatively new to me. I shot my first roll of film in November 2024, after buying my first analogue camera, a Canon A-1, simply to give film photography a try. I quickly became fascinated by the process, and since then, it has become a much bigger part of my life than I initially expected. In fact, I just shot my 100th roll of film during my recent trip to Helsinki.

I remember using simple film cameras as a kid, but once digital cameras became the norm, I assumed film photography had become a thing of the past. Then one day, Instagram's algorithm showed me some analogue photographs while I was scrolling, and I was genuinely surprised to discover that film was still very much alive. I immediately thought, “This is something I have to try.” I did some research and found a basic and affordable analogue camera that I could buy second-hand. The moment I got my first roll developed and saw the results, I was completely hooked. Since then, I’ve been carrying a film camera with me almost everywhere I go.

Looking back, I think the timing was no coincidence. Around the time I started shooting film, I was going through one of the most difficult periods of my life. I was still processing the loss of my parents while also navigating the breakdown of a deeply meaningful yet emotionally very challenging relationship. This chapter of my life was both very painful and transformative.

Wandering the streets of Budapest with a film camera gradually became a way to reconnect with myself, my surroundings, and the people around me. What started as a simple experiment turned into something much more meaningful. Film photography became both a therapeutic outlet and a constant source of joy, and today I honestly can't imagine my life without it.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

So, what were your initial impressions when shooting with your first Lomography rolls?

When you contacted me about this collaboration, I did some research because, to be honest, I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from Lomography films.

When I received the scans from my first Lomography Color Negative 400 roll, I was amazed. The photos turned out great! I loved the colors, the fine grain, the exposure latitude, and the overall feel of the images. Since then, I have already shot another roll of this stock, and I think it will become one of the film stocks I regularly use from now on.

“Film photography became both a therapeutic outlet and a constant source of joy, and today I honestly can't imagine my life without it.”

As for the LomoChrome Purple roll, I had already read about it and seen some photos taken with this stock, so I knew it was an experimental film that could produce some very unique and unexpected results. However, I was still really excited to see what I could create with it, and I was very happy with how the images turned out on my first try.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Using LomoChrome Purple can lead to surprising results. Did you keep the color shifts in mind while shooting?

Yes, definitely. Before using LomoChrome Purple, I had read that it tends to turn greens into purples and blues into shades of turquoise, so I wanted to make sure I had plenty of those colors in my frames. It was interesting to approach the scenes with an idea of what might happen to the colors, while still leaving room for the film to surprise me.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

We hope you are a music fan, too. We're curious – what song would serve best as a soundtrack for shooting on LomoChrome Purple?

Fun fact: I am almost always listening to music when I'm out shooting. I’m pretty sure I was listening to either sombr or a new Hungarian band called Imago Mundi while shooting this roll.

As for what would make the perfect soundtrack for shooting on LomoChrome Purple, I think it really depends on your personal taste. Anything that puts you in the right mood, helps you get into the flow, and sets the pace for your shooting would probably be the perfect soundtrack for you. For me, the music is part of the whole experience.

“I cherish every frame I shoot, even the unsuccessful ones. My first roll probably contains some of my worst photographs, but it is still the most precious roll I have because that is where everything started for me.”

Out of the two rolls, which photo stands out as your favorite?

That's a tough question, but I think I would choose the photo I took under a bridge as a couple happened to walk past me. If you look at their shadows on the wall behind them, their hands meet on the wall even though they aren't actually touching. I really like that little coincidence. It gives the photo an unexpected sense of connection, and I think that's what makes it stand out to me.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

When out with a film camera, what scenes catch your attention the most?

I really appreciate this question. Since I'm still learning and experimenting, I usually have an idea of what I would like to look for when I go out shooting. At the same time, most of my photography happens on the streets of Budapest, and since I have a regular 9-5, I can't always follow those plans. Over time, I have developed a sort of photographic routine: I take my camera with me during my daily commute and photograph whatever catches my attention, while also working on more deliberate projects whenever an idea pops into my head.

In general, I am particularly drawn to candid scenes with some kind of emotional charge. I like moments that feel spontaneous or tell a small story, even if it is not immediately obvious what that story is. At the same time, I enjoy composing images on the spot and experimenting with different techniques just to see what happens. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't, but I think that experimentation is an important part of how I learn.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Have you noticed a strong analogue community in Hungary? Or do you feel like an odd one out with the film gear in your hands?

Since I am still relatively new to analogue street photography and have mostly been learning on my own, I don't feel that I have an accurate picture of the analogue community in Hungary. I have managed to connect online with a few local photographers through Instagram who are interested in analogue photography, but I would say the community is still much smaller than the broader photographer and content creator community.

It is also difficult to define what the “analogue community” actually means. Someone might shoot a roll of film occasionally without necessarily sharing the same passion for the medium as someone who shoots it regularly and is deeply invested in the process.

I actually get a good sense of this from the local lab where I have had almost all of my film developed. They know my name by now and recognize me as a regular customer who comes in several times a week. Once, they mentioned that they appreciated the fact that I always come back for my negatives and that I buy archival materials to store them in, because many of their customers either ask for their negatives to be discarded after development and scanning or simply never come back to collect them.

To me, that is almost painful to hear. I could never throw away my negatives. I cherish every frame I shoot, even the unsuccessful ones. My first roll probably contains some of my worst photographs, but it is still the most precious roll I have because that is where everything started for me.

So, after carrying an analogue camera with me almost everywhere since November 2024, I would say I have mostly felt like an odd one out. But every now and then I spot someone else carrying a film camera, and I've also had people approach me to compliment my camera or ask me a few questions about it. Sometimes people simply tell me that I have a cute camera, which I find both funny and nice at the same time. Those little encounters are always a pleasant reminder that I'm not quite as alone with my film camera as I sometimes feel.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Being a street photographer, what country would you like to visit the most with your camera?

My dream destination has always been the United States, and particularly New York. I had the chance to visit in 2022, but that was before I started shooting analogue street photography, so I had my digital camera with me and approached the city very differently. Some of the photographs I took there are still among my favorites, but looking back, I sometimes wish I had rediscovered film a little earlier so I could have had at least a few analogue photographs from that trip.

New York is my favorite city, and I also see it as one of the great centers of street photography in the world, so I would really love to go back with an analogue camera this time and shoot a few rolls on those streets. I am hoping to return next year, probably in the fall. I don't mind that my second visit will be about five years after my first trip to the United States. By then, I will have had much more time to learn, experiment, and develop my skills. Hopefully, when I return to New York with a film camera, I will be able to see the city differently and come home with even better photographs.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

We see you're experimenting with double exposures, are there any new techniques that you would like to try out?

I absolutely love double and multiple exposures, and I really enjoy experimenting with this technique. It is relatively simple, but it can produce such interesting and unexpected results, which makes it a lot of fun. Film swaps are another type of experiment that I really enjoy. In fact, I recently completed a film swap with another analogue photographer, and the results were great. We’ve already had the roll developed and scanned, and we have even shared some of the images we created together, which made the whole experience even more rewarding.

© Peter Seljan | Shot on Lomography Color Negative 400

I've also experimented with shutter drag, and I definitely want to explore that technique further. But my most recent experimental project was a film soup. That project took almost two months from start to finish, but I finally received the negatives and scans at the end of July, and I was really happy with how the results turned out. And, of course, I couldn't stop there. I've already worked out the recipe for my next film soup project, so there is definitely more experimentation coming.

© Peter Seljan

How about the gear? Is there another Lomography stock or camera on your wish list?

There are a few Lomography film stocks I would like to try next: Lomography Color Negative ISO 800, LomoChrome Color '92 ISO 400, and LomoChrome Metropolis. I have been looking at these on the Lomography website, and they all look very promising to me. I can't wait to see how they perform and what kind of images I can create with them.

As for cameras, I would really like to try a Fisheye camera, because that could be a lot of fun. I am also considering trying a Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera. This is one of the things I love most about analogue photography. There are so many different film stocks, techniques, cameras, and other things to experiment with and learn about. It feels like a never-ending learning curve, but it’s one filled with joy, experimentation, and rewarding images and memories that you can keep.

Check out Peter Seljan's Instagram for more analogue inspiration!
